issues.title: [Dots] Recent cloud-workspace files unavailable after execution stall; older files remain and filesystem identity changes

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

labels.name: dots
labels.description: Issues involving setting up ChatGPT dots or managing their ongoing work.

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

This incident affected the dot’s own cloud execution environment while I was communicating through ChatGPT on the web. I do not have a verified desktop app or backend execution-service version for the incident.

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro. Exact plan tier can be supplied privately if needed.

### What platform is your computer?

Client: Windows, using ChatGPT in a web browser. Affected execution host: OpenAI-hosted Linux cloud computer belonging to my dot. The affected files and test were not running on my Windows laptop or Mac.

### What issue are you seeing?

Summary
I’m reporting a recurring loss of accessible working state on my dot’s cloud computer. During the latest incident, filesystem operations stalled while an offline software test was running. The execution service subsequently disconnected. When command access returned, recent source worktrees, Git history locations and test evidence were missing, while older project files remained.
Reported filesystem usage fell from roughly 30 GB to 3.3 GB. This includes build caches, binaries and generated test artifacts; it should not be interpreted as 26 GB of unique source code or proof of permanent physical deletion.
I did not click Pause, Reboot, Delete or Reset, or otherwise interact with the cloud environment during the incident. The observations below come from commands run by my assistant and retained conversation/tool results, not OpenAI backend logs.
Environment
- Product: ChatGPT dots, using the dot’s own Linux cloud computer
- Client used for this conversation: Windows web browser
- Workload: offline Rust software development and verification, with separate implementation and review workers
- Working files: task scratch and shared workspace directories
- User’s Windows laptop and Mac were not executing the affected test
- This was not an ordinary temporary data-analysis session or a repository-backed Codex Cloud task
- Exact frontend and execution-service versions were not captured
Observed timeline
All times are UTC on October 10, 2026.
- 02:24:37: An end-to-end offline test started against a pinned source revision. Thirteen focused author tests had passed before this run
- 02:33:43: The last observed database progress recorded allocation of an output copy. The test had already passed several reader-selection, stale/corrupt-source and interrupted-write retry checks
- Around 02:35: Separate workers began encountering stalled filesystem operations, including simple file inspection and directory listing. These were not limited to the product test
- 02:38: A filesystem check still reported approximately 30 GB used, with only about 183 MB available. The current source revision and running-test receipt were still readable
- 02:55:03: The current kernel’s boot time, read after access returned. This does not independently establish the previous kernel’s identity or the exact moment the task was attached to a different environment
- Around 02:58: Attempts to resume existing execution sessions returned: “exec-server transport disconnected; failed to resume exec-server session: recovery timed out after 25s”
- Around 03:01: Commands from a temporary directory worked again. The original top-level working directory existed, but recent implementation worktrees and the latest test receipt were absent. Reported filesystem usage was approximately 3.3 GB
- Subsequent read-only inspection found older pre-code and unrelated files, but not the recent implementation trees, verification directories or runtime test roots previously used by the task
The interrupted test has no observed final exit status. Its result remains unknown and has not been credited as passing.
Evidence of a filesystem or environment transition
1. Changed overlay identity
An environment record recovered from an externally saved, manifest-verified archive identifies an earlier overlay mount. The current mount has a different identifier. This supports a change in the presented filesystem environment; it does not identify whether the mechanism was replacement, restoration, reassociation or another lifecycle operation.
2. Recent metadata timestamps on older files
Several surviving directories have metadata-change timestamps around 03:01 UTC, while retaining older modification timestamps, including October 5 dates. This is consistent with files being restored or rematerialized, but ctime is not a creation timestamp and does not establish the snapshot’s age.
3. Missing state across multiple categories
The disappearance affected source worktrees, Git-history locations, test receipts, build outputs and runtime roots. A stopped test process alone would not explain those missing directories.
4. Low available storage before the incident
The earlier filesystem had approximately 183 MB available. This is relevant diagnostic context. We have not established that disk exhaustion caused the stall or transition, and no captured ENOSPC error establishes that explanation.
5. Diagnostic limits
Kernel logs were inaccessible. Counters read from the current kernel cannot rule out an out-of-memory or other failure in a previous environment. The assistant cannot inspect platform-side lifecycle, storage-association or snapshot logs.
Cleanup actions and scope
The assistant had previously removed explicitly bounded generated metadata and redundant caches. Those recorded removals were far smaller than the observed usage change, excluded original source and verification receipts, and were followed by successful builds, focused tests and the subsequent running test.
These recorded cleanup actions do not explain the broad disappearance of recent source and evidence. However, this report is not an assertion that every platform action or filesystem operation has been audited; that requires backend records.
Earlier incident on the same dot
This is not my first experience of missing work in this conversation. Before the current incident, we had already discussed missing research progress, including what I described as 12–14 research cycles/runs.
That earlier event led me to request backups on my laptop and regular ZIP checkpoints explicitly. My instructions included saving everything so another environment loss would not erase the work, and continuing to send ZIPs periodically.
The earlier incident’s exact onset, filesystem identifiers and complete loss inventory are not established in this report. Please correlate it with the earlier activity in the same dot conversation. I am reporting recurrence of the user-visible problem, not claiming that both incidents have a proven common cause.
Impact and recovery
- Recent source changes and verification evidence became inaccessible, interrupting development and independent acceptance
- External Library backups survived and matched their recorded SHA-256 hashes
- Those backups allowed recovery of an earlier accepted repository baseline and a later in-progress source snapshot
- Source changes and receipts created after the latest saved snapshot have not been recovered from the currently accessible workspace or available backup chain
- Some lost evidence will require genuine re-execution; remembered results cannot replace missing acceptance receipts
- The assistant also allowed newer changes to accumulate locally while waiting for a verified checkpoint. That backup gap increased the recovery cost, but does not explain the environment transition
After I requested investigation before further recovery, the recovery job already in flight finished in a new directory. No coding, builds or tests have resumed.
Expected behavior
OpenAI’s guide says the cloud computer “can keep its state between periods of use”: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots/computers-and-apps
I understand that this wording does not define a complete durability guarantee. However, an ongoing development task needs a clear persistence contract: which paths survive, what events can replace state, how recent a restored snapshot should be, and how users are warned when work is at risk.
An unexpected transition should preserve recoverable work or clearly report what happened and how to retrieve the previous state.
Reproduction status
There is no deterministic reproduction. We have not deliberately rebooted, reset or filled the filesystem to reproduce this issue. The observed sequence was active work → stalled filesystem calls → execution disconnect → renewed access with recent files missing and older files present.

Requested investigation
1. Correlate this dot and execution session with the environment and storage history during approximately 02:35–03:01 UTC on October 10
2. Identify what caused the filesystem stalls and subsequent execution-service disconnect
3. Determine whether the task was attached to a replacement environment, an older snapshot, a different writable layer or another storage association
4. Preserve and locate the preceding writable layer and any newer snapshots before cleanup makes recovery harder
5. Confirm whether the missing source changes and evidence can be recovered
6. Explain the supported persistence guarantees for task scratch and shared workspace directories
7. Explain low-disk-space behavior, including whether it can trigger replacement or restoration and what warnings or recovery mechanisms exist
8. Clarify exactly what Pause and Reboot affect, including delegated tasks, active processes, filesystem state and snapshots
9. Correlate the earlier reported loss in this same dot conversation without assuming a common cause
10. Provide a supported method for durable, automatic checkpoints outside the execution filesystem
Privacy
This public draft omits account details, private project contents, full private paths, conversation/session identifiers and exact environment identifiers. Relevant correlation details and available diagnostic hashes can be supplied through an appropriate private support channel.
Current conclusion
Recent working state is demonstrably missing from the accessible environment, and the observed filesystem identity differs from an earlier verified record. The underlying cause and recoverability of the previous storage remain unresolved. Please investigate before treating this as an ordinary task interruption or user-initiated reset.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

No deterministic reproduction is available. The observed sequence was:
1. Continue an existing development task on the dot’s cloud computer, with source worktrees, Git history, test evidence and external Library checkpoints
2. Start an offline test against a pinned source revision at 02:24:37 UTC on October 10, 2026
3. Observe filesystem operations stall around 02:35, including independent file inspection and directory listing
4. Receive execution-service transport disconnection and recovery-timeout errors around 02:58
5. When commands work again around 03:01, inspect the original workspace paths
6. Find recent source and verification directories absent, older files still present, and reported filesystem usage reduced from approximately 30 GB to 3.3 GB
7. Compare diagnostics: the current overlay identifier differs from an earlier hash-verified environment record
I did not click Pause, Reboot, Delete or Reset. We have not deliberately reproduced the incident through rebooting or filling the disk. Available storage was low before the failure, but causation is unproven. The interrupted test’s final outcome is unknown. Private session identifiers can be supplied to support; token and context-window usage were not captured.

### What is the expected behavior?

Previously saved project files should remain accessible within the cloud computer’s supported persistence scope. If the platform replaces an environment or restores a snapshot, it should preserve recoverable work, disclose the transition and snapshot age, and provide recovery guidance.
Please clarify which directories persist, what events can discard or replace their state, and what happens when disk space becomes low. A running development task should not silently return to an older accessible state without a clear warning or recovery path.

### Additional information

This is a recurring user-visible issue in the same dot conversation. An earlier incident involved missing research progress described as 12–14 cycles/runs and led to explicit requests for frequent ZIP and laptop backups. Its exact cause and timing are not established here.
External Library backups survived this incident and were hash-verified. They recovered an accepted baseline and later in-progress work. Four subsequent repair areas, including eleven focused tests and later local-only verification records, remain absent from the recovered source/evidence set. Build caches and generated artifacts account for part of the disk-usage difference; we are not claiming 26 GB of unique source was permanently deleted.
Please preserve and investigate the preceding writable layer and snapshots, correlate environment/storage transitions during October 10, 02:35–03:01 UTC, and establish whether newer work is recoverable. Exact identifiers can be provided privately. No backend root cause has been established.

- FlClash TUN mode, mixed stack; observed model traffic routes through a manually selected proxy
- Latest-version status is unverified: the read-only updater reports that Windows Store eligibility requires a potentially downloading Store check, which was not started.

### Observed behavior
The user identifies historical images in a specific ongoing local chat as failing. At 2026-10-07 05:14:04.321 UTC, immediately after thread/read and thread/items/list activity for that chat, desktop logs contain:

```text
warning [electron-message-handler] sa_server_request_failed
method=get
routePattern=/files/download/{file_id}
```

This confirms one empty-identifier image download failure. It does not prove that every missing image has the same cause, or map this exact request to a particular image tile.

### Data-preservation check
Read-only inspection of the affected chat's durable local rollout found embedded image bytes. Extraction with SHA-256 deduplication recovered 436 distinct images (102,784,448 bytes), including tool previews/screenshots and input images. All 436 passed full Pillow decoding. The aggregate is not a count of broken tiles, and does not establish that every missing image is present.

The original rollout, databases, app package and project files were not modified.

### Packaged-code inspection / debugging lead
Read-only inspection of the installed webview bundle (app-initial-7ad941570eaa.js) found:
- i7t strips file-service:// or sediment:// prefixes and otherwise passes the string through.
- c7t passes the result to p7t for the Codex resolver.
- p7t calls /files/download/{file_id} without its own nonempty-ID check.
- a7t normally gates the query with enabled = ... && !!e, but its returned refetch callback calls the query refetch without an explicit nonempty-pointer guard.
- o7t also directly invokes fetchQuery(s7t(...)).

These are investigation leads, NOT a proven upstream root cause or a verified patch. We did not establish which caller supplied the empty pointer, and merely suppressing the invalid request would not restore the image.

### Expected behavior
Historical images with retained image data should render in the original conversation. Inline/local image data must not be resolved via an empty cloud file ID. If a reference genuinely cannot be resolved, the app should explain why and offer a supported recovery path.

### Requested investigation
Please investigate the historical-image normalization/resolver path, including retry behavior with empty pointers, and provide a supported repair or fixed build that preserves existing local chats and active work.

Potentially related but distinct: #43153 involves a composite sediment reference and Invalid file_id; #34801 involves a nonempty reference and a 403 authorization failure. This report's observed error is an EMPTY reference and HTTP 422 No file_id provided.

No private conversation titles/IDs, image contents, credentials, full logs, proxy endpoint addresses, or user paths are included.

issues.title: Browser Use Node REPL fails in Windows Desktop app with WSL workspace due to unmapped sandboxCwd

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: mcp
labels.description: Issues related to the use of model context protocol (MCP) servers

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
## Summary

Browser Use / Node REPL does not work in the Codex Windows Desktop app when the agent is configured to run in WSL and the project lives on the WSL filesystem. The Desktop app auto-generates a `node_repl` MCP server that runs a Windows `node_repl.exe`, but tool calls send a Linux/WSL `sandboxCwd` URI (`file:///home/...`). The Windows-side Node REPL rejects that path as not being a local file URI.

All paths below are anonymized.

## Environment

- Codex Desktop app on Windows
- Agent configured to run in WSL2
- Integrated terminal configured as WSL
- WSL distro: Ubuntu 22.04
- Project path inside WSL: `/home/<user>/projects/<repo>`
- Windows view of same project: `\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-22.04\home\<user>\projects\<repo>`
- `CODEX_HOME` inside the WSL agent session: `/mnt/c/Users/<windows-user>/.codex`
- Codex CLI from `codex doctor`: `Codex Doctor v0.142.0 · linux-x86_64`
- Desktop/browser runtime version visible in generated MCP env: `BROWSER_USE_CODEX_APP_VERSION=26.616.71553`
- Browser Use plugin enabled

Relevant config state:

```toml
[desktop]
runCodexInWindowsSubsystemForLinux = true
integratedTerminalShell = "wsl"

[plugins."browser-use@openai-bundled"]
enabled = true
```

## Reproduction Steps

1. On Windows, configure Codex Desktop to run the agent in WSL.
2. Open a project located on the WSL filesystem, e.g. `/home/<user>/projects/<repo>`.
3. Enable the Browser Use plugin.
4. Start/restart Codex Desktop.
5. Inspect MCP configuration from the WSL agent session:

```bash
codex mcp get node_repl
```

Codex Desktop auto-generates a user-level MCP server similar to:

```toml
[mcp_servers.node_repl]
command = "/mnt/c/Users/<windows-user>/AppData/Local/OpenAI/Codex/runtimes/cua_node/<runtime-id>/bin/node_repl.exe"
startup_timeout_sec = 120

[mcp_servers.node_repl.env]
BROWSER_USE_AVAILABLE_BACKENDS = "chrome"
CODEX_HOME = "C:\\Users\\<windows-user>\\.codex"
CODEX_CLI_PATH = "/usr/local/bin/codex"
WSLENV = "..."
```

6. Trigger a Node REPL JS call, for example through Browser Use setup or directly via the exposed `node_repl/js` tool.

## Actual Behavior

The Node REPL tool is visible, but every JS execution fails immediately:

```text
tool call failed for `node_repl/js`

Caused by:
    Mcp error: -32602: js: codex/sandbox-state-meta: sandboxCwd is not a local file URI: file:///home/<user>/projects/<repo>
```

This blocks Browser Use entirely. The in-app browser cannot be automated from Codex in this setup.

## Expected Behavior

When the Desktop app is configured to run the agent in WSL, Browser Use should work for WSL-hosted projects. Either:

- the `node_repl` MCP process should run in the matching WSL/Linux environment, or
- Codex should map the WSL sandbox cwd to a Windows-local/UNC path before passing it to a Windows-side `node_repl.exe`, e.g. `\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-22.04\home\<user>\projects\<repo>`, or
- Browser Use should provision its internal Node REPL / backend in a way that does not mix Windows runtime expectations with Linux `file:///home/...` sandbox metadata.

## Additional Diagnostics

`codex doctor --summary` from the WSL agent session confirms the agent/runtime is Linux/WSL:

```text
Codex Doctor v0.142.0 · linux-x86_64
Environment: Ubuntu 22.04, WSL_DISTRO_NAME present
Configuration: config loaded from /mnt/c/Users/<windows-user>/.codex/config.toml
MCP: 1 server (1 stdio)
Sandbox: restricted fs + restricted network
```

`codex mcp get node_repl` confirms the generated MCP server uses a Windows executable:

```text
command: /mnt/c/Users/<windows-user>/AppData/Local/OpenAI/Codex/runtimes/cua_node/<runtime-id>/bin/node_repl.exe
cwd: -
```

I also tested adding an explicit UNC cwd to the generated MCP block:

```toml
cwd = '\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-22.04\home\<user>\projects\<repo>'
```

Codex accepted and displayed that cwd via `codex mcp get node_repl`, but the tool still failed with the same `sandboxCwd is not a local file URI: file:///home/...` error. After restarting Codex Desktop, the generated MCP block was overwritten again and the explicit `cwd` was removed.

I also tested disabling the Chrome and Computer Use plugins while keeping Browser Use enabled. Codex Desktop still regenerated the same Windows `node_repl.exe` MCP block with `BROWSER_USE_AVAILABLE_BACKENDS = "chrome"`.

I did not use `--disable-sandbox`; this report is about the default sandboxed path.

### Summary
After Codex native Computer Use operates a macOS application, a human pressing a physical key once can produce two characters (a → aa). This persists after the agent stops operating. A single native-control session is sufficient.

### Environment
- macOS 26.6.2 (25G83)
- Desktop client: 26.1027.30824, bundle build 22943
- SkyComputerUseService: 26.1022.1001641 (1001641)
- Confirmed target: Feishu/Lark desktop
- Reproduces with the macOS ABC input source, so it is not limited to Chinese IME composition

### Reproduction observed
1. Start one native Computer Use session and bind Feishu using cua.getApp("Lark").
2. Read fresh application state, then use app.pressKey("super+k") to open the search field.
3. The human user physically taps a once. The field receives aa.
4. Reset only the cua_repl session with js_reset. The user now gets one a per physical press, without restarting the target app, main client, or helper service.

### Diagnostic observations
CGGetEventTapList showed two enabled, non-listen-only keyboard taps owned by SkyComputerUseService targeting the same Feishu process; both subscribed to keyDown/keyUp/flagsChanged. These taps disappeared after the session reset while the helper remained running. This is evidence to investigate, not proof that duplicate registration alone causes the duplicate delivery.

Stopping only the helper also restored normal typing in an earlier controlled test. The user reports that stopping the agent task alone was insufficient, while quitting the client restored input.

### Browser scope
The user previously experienced similar browser symptoms around the same period. However, a fresh Chrome about:blank/address-bar test on 2026-10-30 did **not** reproduce duplication. The confirmed reproduction above is in the native Feishu app; browser history remains unconfirmed.

### Expected behavior
Physical user keystrokes should be delivered exactly once during and after automation, without manually resetting sessions or stopping services. Please investigate native event forwarding/source tagging and event-tap lifecycle. This report concerns the desktop Computer Use component rather than ordinary CLI terminal input.

Observed on 2026-10-30 (Asia/Shanghai). No private application content or raw logs are included.

issues.title: [Windows][Computer Use] zh-CN document-role URL detection failure on @oai/sky 0.7.8; narrow correction restores Chrome and Edge

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
## Summary

On Chinese-language Windows, native Computer Use could enumerate and activate Chrome/Edge windows, but acquiring Chrome window state stopped with the browser-URL confidence error. On this installation, a narrowly scoped document-type predicate correction in the native helper restored native window-state acquisition and browser interaction in both Chrome and Edge.

This adds a verified **@oai/sky 0.7.8 / zh-CN** result to #53026, whose published local repair was originally restricted to a different 0.7.7 helper hash. Please ship an official source-level correction rather than requiring users to patch signed executables.

Related reports:
- #53026 — localized document-role comparison and Korean before/after evidence.
- #25271 — native browser URL detection failure.
- #54490 — my earlier extension-sidepanel report. This issue concerns the native Windows Computer Use path, not the sidepanel iframe/CSP path.

## Environment verified on 2026-10-16

| Component | Version |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | Windows 11 Home, build 26300; UI culture zh-CN |
| Desktop app | 26.1013.31256, build 20586 |
| Installed MSIX | 26.1013.3656.0 |
| Computer Use bundle | 26.1013.31256 |
| @oai/sky | 0.7.8 |
| Chrome | 155.0.8059.84 |
| Microsoft Edge | 155.0.4283.45 |

The desktop updater returned `up_to_date` before the local correction. The original native helper had a valid OpenAI OpCo, LLC Authenticode signature.

## Failure before the correction

Using the documented `@oai/sky` API:

1. Enumerate windows with `sky.list_windows()`.
2. Select the unique Chrome window returned by the API.
3. Bind it with `sky.get_window()` and activate it.
4. Request window state.

A fresh Chrome New Tab failed before a usable screenshot/accessibility tree was returned:

```text
Computer Use has been stopped for this turn because it could not determine the current browser URL on Windows with enough confidence to enforce policy.
```

Native input was not continued after that stop. The later validation occurred after explicit user authorization for the local correction.

## Local correction and integrity checks

The helper is located under:

```text
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\<runtime>\bin\node_modules\@oai\sky\bin\windows\codex-computer-use.exe
```

Original SHA-256:

```text
14d5e9c7336dd34aa8476f218dd45e033b8416bdad6c58fa79c84169ae59f2f3
```

The complete original 42-byte predicate sequence from [heelee912/codex commit 95ee61d](https://github.com/heelee912/codex/commit/95ee61db4a387944889edc9a5b6e97272c8fca9d) occurred exactly once in this 0.7.8 file, at the same file offset, `0x1B6C6`.

The published script was **not** run with its hash guard disabled. Instead, this installation's original whole-file hash, the exact original instruction sequence, its uniqueness, and its offset were checked before a local adaptation.

The correction replaces the localized-role string predicate with:

```text
successful CachedControlType read
AND CachedControlType == UIA_DocumentControlTypeId (50030)
```

A failed getter or a non-document type follows the non-candidate path. The later RootWebArea/value checks and all bytes outside the 42-byte region were left unchanged. This does not inject a URL, force a successful policy result, or disable URL/permission enforcement.

Validation of the file modification:
- Original file backed up and backup SHA-256 verified.
- 42-byte region replaced; 36 bytes actually differ.
- Complete modified file read back and compared with the expected image.
- No changes outside that region.

Modified SHA-256:

```text
08a7a2a9b94ef1c63b935d0424c04289fffbef8c766cab7b7cde67ab68c0f277
```

As expected, modifying the signed executable makes Authenticode report `HashMismatch`. This is an unsupported local workaround, not an official signed fix. No binaries are attached or distributed.

## Actual native Computer Use results afterward

Validation used `@oai/sky` native APIs, not extension-backed Browser Use as a substitute.

| Check | Chrome | Edge |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Native accessibility tree and screenshot returned | Passed | Passed |
| Navigate through the native address-bar control to the public Selenium web form | Passed | Passed |
| Click the Text input control | Passed | Passed after refreshing window/geometry |
| Set test text through native `sky.set_value` | Passed | Passed |
| Read back the exact text in the native tree and screenshot | Passed | Passed |
| Clear test text and restore the original New Tab page | Passed | Passed |

No browser-URL confidence error recurred during these checks. Screenshot-plus-text and text-only state requests succeeded. Screenshot-only requests were not separately tested.

Ordinary minimized-window, user-input-detected, and one click-geometry precondition occurred during validation and were handled by fresh observation/activation. Those checks were not disabled. Some structured `focused_element` results still referred to the address bar after a click, so this report does not claim that every native focus/geometry issue is resolved. Writing was verified through an explicitly targeted native control and actual content readback.

## Scope and limitations

- This is before/after evidence for this particular installation and predicate change, not proof that every report with this error has the same cause.
- We did not instrument the live UIA getter values on this machine, nor perform a full restore/reapply runtime experiment.
- Persistence across a complete desktop restart or a future update has not been tested; updates may replace the local correction.
- A separate browser-tool networking problem was resolved by routing the tool process through the configured proxy. Extension-backed page reading/writing worked before the native correction. Proxy success alone did not repair the native URL failure.

## Requested upstream fix

Please:
1. Classify document controls using successful numeric ControlType reads rather than localized display text.
2. Preserve the existing URL parsing, window identity, candidate validation, and access-policy enforcement.
3. Cover zh-CN/ko-KR and other localized document names, non-document controls named "document", and getter failures in regression tests.
4. Link the official source-level fix and the first signed desktop/runtime release containing it.

Only public test-page details and component metadata are included; no private page contents, account details, screenshots, user-specific paths, or raw logs are attached.

issues.body: ### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)? 26.1016.51333 ### What subscription do you have? plus ### What platform is your computer? Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64 ### What issue are you seeing? Running Codex Desktop over a period of time causes a severe system-wide kernel memory leak. This results in Windows Nonpaged Pool memory exhaustion, system stuttering, and eventual OOM (Out of Memory) behavior. The leak persists even after completely exiting the application and requires a full system reboot to clear. I used Sysinternals PoolMon (poolmon.exe -b) to monitor kernel pool tags over a 30-minute period. The data clearly isolates Codex Desktop as the trigger and the NtFc tag (associated with ntfs.sys file object creation) as the culprit. While Codex is running, the NtFc (Nonpaged) tag grows continuously and massively. - Avail Memory: Dropped from ~8.8 GB to ~1.3 GB. - Nonpaged Pool: Inflated to over 14.2 GB. - NtFc Bytes: Grew from ~11.31 GB to ~11.88 GB, with the Diff (unfreed allocations) climbing to over 40,000,000. Immediately after exiting Codex, the leak instantly stops, confirming Codex is the trigger. However, the leaked memory is not released. The NtFc Bytes remain stuck at ~12.92 GB, and the Diff freezes at ~40,551,986. Two minutes after exiting Codex, the leaked memory remains completely static. ### What steps can reproduce the bug? 1. Launch Codex Desktop. 2. Use the application normally (triggering file scanning/indexing, code completion, etc.). 3. Keep the system running for 30-60 minutes. 4. Monitor the system memory using Task Manager or RAMMap. The "Nonpaged Pool" will steadily grow until the system becomes unresponsive. 5. Close Codex Desktop completely. The memory will not be released; a full system reboot is required to recover the RAM. ### What is the expected behavior? When Codex Desktop performs file system operations, it should properly release handles and references. Closing the application should terminate all related background processes and release the allocated kernel memory. ### Additional information Technical Analysis: NtFc is the pool tag used by the NTFS file system driver (ntfs.sys) when creating file objects. It is highly likely that Codex Desktop's high-frequency file system operations (such as git ls-files spawning thousands of sub-processes, or continuous scanning of cache directories like GrShaderCache) are causing ntfs.sys to allocate file objects that are never properly freed (reference count leak). Temporary Workarounds: Restarting the computer completely (Note: "Fast Startup" must be disabled, or a "Restart" must be used instead of "Shut Down"). Clearing/Renaming Codex cache directories (like GrShaderCache) upon exit.

prs.title: Persist subagent relationships before creating child storage
prs.body:
Persist subagent relationships before creating child storage

## Why

Creating child history before persisting its parent-child relationship can leave history that parent subtree deletion cannot discover, especially when fork startup copies history. A relationship write failure must reject the spawn before child storage is created.

## What changed

- Reserve the child thread ID and persist its spawn edge before starting the child. Propagate persistence failures to the caller.
- Keep pending relationship writes owned through caller cancellation, and wait for them to finish before closing the edge during cleanup, including when a write commits but reports an error.
- Skip edge cleanup when publication was skipped, and reject IDs belonging to running threads before publication.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for cancellation before commit or acknowledgement, errors after commit, skipped publication, and duplicate child IDs. Integration tests cover fresh children and full-history forks, verifying that failed publication leaves no child history, execution, or creation notification and preserves unrelated history during parent deletion.

prs.title: Add trace-safe diagnostics for Noise relay request progress
prs.body:
Add trace-safe diagnostics for Noise relay request progress

## Why

WebSocket heartbeat progress only establishes relay reachability, not executor receipt or completion. A blocked write or full application queue can also leave a Pong unread, so diagnosing stalled requests requires separate transport and application progress signals.

## What changed

- Trace request dequeue and completed writes under the request's trace context, and emit an executor receipt span immediately after decoding, before queueing or execution completes.
- Record RPC enqueue wait time and queue occupancy.
- Add bounded heartbeat events and a transport closure summary with fixed exit categories, queue depths, message counters, and read/write timing. Distinguish write timeouts from missing Pongs and report application delivery backpressure separately.
- Keep request methods, IDs, payloads, raw errors, and peer-provided text out of the new trace-safe transport diagnostics.

## Testing

Add coverage for blocked data and keepalive writes, missing Pongs, saturated application queues, read errors, and responsive relays without application responses. Verify trace correlation, immediate receipt span export, bounded Pong telemetry, and exclusion of payloads and raw error text.

labels.name: priority/p2

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
**Goal:** To significantly improve the reliability, visibility, and actionability of our project's internal (non-benchmark) evaluations.

**Problem:** Our current small project evals are inconsistent ("bleed"), making it difficult to trust their results, track quality trends, and quickly address regressions. This slows down development and impacts confidence in changes.

**Vision:** A streamlined evaluation system where internal project evals are stable, provide clear signals, and enable rapid feedback loops. Developers can confidently rely on these evals to catch issues early and understand the impact of their changes.

**Key Outcomes:**

- Reduced flakiness and increased reliability of existing project evals.
- Clear visibility into eval results and historical trends.
- Faster detection and easier debugging of regressions.
- Basic automation to flag issues and guide developers.
- "Approve" button to increase visibility and reduce excessive runs

**Out of Scope:**

- Large-scale benchmark evals (e.g., SWE-bench, terminal-bench).
- Overhauling the entire testing infrastructure beyond the scope of these specific project evals.

labels.name: priority/p2

labels.description: Issues that were reported by customers

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

issues.body:
In certain cases, the main agent spends many turns, iterations, making incremental changes in hopes of solving a small issue. For example, if a typecheck or linter comes back with numerous failures. The main agent may spend many turns/tokens to help get the build into a healthy state. 

This is one such subtask (also including fixing a broken build) that could be delegated to a subagent such as the generalist to outsource the fix and return to the main agent with a working build. 

Considerations/Objectives:
- Investigate getting the model to use the generalist in subtasks such as this
- evaluate if calling is consistent and provides enough feedback back to the main agent to prevent any hallucinations of state (does the generalist let the main agent know what changes it had to make / if the fix couldn't be fixed without further changes)
- Does the main agent provide enough context for the generalist to successfully accomplish its tasks? Or could this require a way for the main agent to share more context?
- Add behavior evals to see if the behavior is followed consistently.

issues.body:
Update the existing review skill to utilize custom subagents + parallel invocation to create a review loop that the main agent (orchestrator) can call. 

The goal here is to have the main agent's work be reviewed by specialized personas that work in parallel to provide high quality feedback and double check work. 

Example iteration:

1. Bug Provided to main agent
2. Main agent plans and implements changes
3. Once the main agent is happy with its changes, it activates a self-review cycle via skill
4. Parallel subagents work to review the complete change and original bug to ensure completeness, correctness, and ensure no regressions.
5. Feedback from subagents is fed back to the main agent to either make corrections or proceed.

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

### What happened?

This is purely anecdotal, but IME Gemini does not use custom skills and sub-agents on its own, basically at all.  It will if I instruct it to explicitly, but won't when it's doing something very related.

For example, I have "gradle" and "git" skills with descriptions like:
> Executes and manages Gradle builds authoritatively with high-performance background orchestration 
  and surgical failure analysis. This skill is the STRONGLY PREFERRED way 
  to run any Gradle task, providing superior reliability through managed background processes, 
  task-specific output capturing, and deep diagnostic integration. Use it for executing core 
  lifecycle tasks like 'build' or 'assemble', starting persistent development servers, 
  or performing complex build troubleshooting. Do NOT use for specialized test diagnostics 
  (use running_gradle_tests).

and 
> Audits Git repository status, examines history, and implements non-interactive modifications. Processes surgical staging, descriptive commits, and multi-file diff analysis. Use for repository introspection and history-based truth verification. NEVER stages or commits without explicit user directives. Avoids interactive prompts via --no-pager.

that never ever get called when using the relevant tools.

I even have this in my `GEMINI.md` in the "priority rules" section:
> 4. **Agent & Tool Hierarchy:** Whenver considering how to approach a task or do anything, ALWAYS follow the hierarchy of preference: **Sub-Agents** > **Skills** > **Specialized MCP Tools** (NOT a Shell tool or similar) > **General/Builtin Tools** (e.g., `run_shell_command`, `grep_search`, `read_file`).
> 5. **Intentionality Protocol:** Before starting ANY task, you MUST stop and consider which agent, skill, or tool is most appropriate for the specific context. If your plan involves using the shell (even via a tool like `run_shell_command`), you MUST stop and reconsider if a more specialized tool or skill exists to handle the task more reliably.

I expected Gemini to use related skills when working on tasks that match the skill description.  Same for sub-agents.

### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. The agent needs strict grounding in its own documentation to accurately guide users.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

issues.title: /compress command is not persistent across session resume

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/small
labels.description: 1 day or less: trivial logic, UI adjustments, docs

issues.body:
### What happened?

The `/compress` command, which summarizes chat history to save tokens, is not persistent across session exits and resumes. When a user runs `/compress`, the in-memory chat history is correctly replaced by a summary, but this change is not written back to the session file on disk. Consequently, when the session is resumed later (using `--resume` or `/resume`), the CLI loads the original, uncompressed history from the session file, effectively losing the compression.

**Repro Steps:**
1. Start a chat with `gemini`.
2. Build up some history with several messages.
3. Run `/compress` and wait for completion.
4. Exit the CLI.
5. Resume the session with `gemini --resume latest`.
6. Observe that the history has reverted to its uncompressed state.

### What did you expect to happen?

Running `/compress` should persist the compressed history (the summary) to the session file on disk so that subsequent resumes of the same session correctly load the compressed state.

### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

OS: darwin (macOS)
Version: Current (detected in local development)

</details>

### Login information

N/A (General bug in persistence logic)

### Anything else we need to know?

Investigation shows that in `packages/core/src/core/client.ts`, the `tryCompressChat` method correctly replaces the `this.chat` object with a new `GeminiChat` initialized with the compressed history:
```typescript
this.chat = await this.startChat(newHistory, resumedData);
```
However, the `ChatRecordingService` (which manages the session file) is initialized with `resumedData` (which points to the existing session file) but is not explicitly instructed to overwrite the file's message history with the new `newHistory`. The `initialize` method in `ChatRecordingService` merely points to the existing file without clearing or updating its messages.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

Linked Draft PR: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/pull/18924

labels.name: priority/p3

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

prs.title: fix(settings): preserve disk edits when changing authentication
prs.body:
## Summary

Preserve settings-file edits made after Gemini CLI starts when a setting, including the authentication method, is saved. Save the requested property against the current disk contents instead of rewriting the startup snapshot.

## Details

Limit property writes to the changed path while retaining unrelated disk additions, deletions, comments, environment placeholders, and array/object changes. If a required ancestor has become incompatible, recreate the ancestors needed for that property while keeping unrelated settings. Object-valued assignments still replace the assigned object. Malformed JSON is reported and left intact.

Document `/auth signin`/`login`, `/auth signout`/`logout`, and normal `/quit` persistence. Opening or cancelling authentication selection does not reset preferences; signout removes the selected authentication type, while normal quit retains saved preferences and credentials. No public settings/schema or package-version changes.

## Related Issues

Related to #23138. Its stale `originalSettings` snapshot also reproduces when changing authentication on the upstream base used here.

prs.title: fix(cli): only auto-nudge genuinely empty continuations and await the nudge
prs.body:
## Summary

When a tool-loop continuation came back with no visible text, `useGeminiStream` automatically sent a nudge (`[System: You successfully executed a tool but returned an empty response...]`). It did this as a fire-and-forget promise from inside the stream loop, and it only checked that the text buffer was empty. As a result the nudge also fired when the stream ended for reasons that are **not** an empty model response, including **after the user pressed Esc**. In that case it silently undid the cancellation and started a new request. This PR only nudges genuinely empty continuations and sequences the nudge properly.

## Details

**Before** (`processGeminiStreamEvents`):

- The nudge condition was just `isContinuation && buffer is empty && attempts < 2`. That is also true when the stream ended with:
  - `UserCancelled`, or a signal aborted by Esc. `submitQuery` then resets `turnCancelledRef` and creates a new `AbortController`, so **the cancel is undone and the model is called again**.
  - `Error`: the error is shown, then another request is sent anyway.
  - `AgentExecutionStopped` / `AgentExecutionBlocked`: a hook asked the agent to stop and the nudge overrode it.
  - `MaxSessionTurns`, `ContextWindowWillOverflow`, `LoopDetected`.
  - `InvalidStream`, e.g. `NO_RESPONSE_TEXT`. Since #28934 the core already retries empty responses with its own nudge (`NO_RESPONSE_TEXT_NUDGE_MESSAGE`) before reporting this, so the CLI nudge was a second, stacked retry.
- The nudge was a floating `submitQueryRef.current?.(...)` call, started before the outer `submitQuery` had flushed its pending history item.

**After:**

- `processGeminiStreamEvents` records when the stream ended abnormally (the events above). It returns a new `StreamProcessingStatus.EmptyContinuation` only for a continuation that ended normally, was not aborted, and produced no text or tool calls.
- `submitQuery` handles that status after flushing the pending history item. It sends the nudge only if:
  - the turn was not cancelled (`turnCancelledRef`),
  - no newer query has started (`activeQueryIdRef`),
  - and the attempt limit is not reached.
- The nudge is **awaited**, so the request stays `Responding` until the nudge has finished.
- The nudge text is unchanged, moved to a module constant. The now-unused `prompt_id` parameter of `processGeminiStreamEvents` is removed.

**Not changed:** the issue also suggests skipping `geminiClient.addHistory` for completed tools in the cancelled path of `handleCompletedTools`. I left that alone. Those responses pair the model's `functionCall` turn that is already in history, and dropping them would leave an unanswered `functionCall`, which is the corruption the surrounding code works to avoid (see the comment in the `modelSwitchedFromQuotaError` branch). Happy to look at it separately if maintainers see a concrete repro.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29071

## How to Validate

```bash
npm run build --workspace @google/gemini-cli-core
cd packages/cli && npx vitest run src/ui/hooks/useGeminiStream.test.tsx -t "nudge"
```

New `auto-nudge on empty continuation responses` tests:

- an always-empty continuation is nudged exactly twice, all sends share the prompt id, and everything has finished by the time the continuation's own promise resolves
- no nudge when the stream ended with: an error, an invalid stream, a hook stopping the agent, a hook blocking the agent, a user cancellation, or the session turn limit
- no nudge when the user cancels (`cancelOngoingRequest`) while the continuation is still streaming

7 of these fail on `main` and pass with this change. The existing auto-nudge test (via `handleCompletedTools`) still passes. All CLI hook and `AppContainer` tests pass (68 files, 1278 tests), and typecheck and lint are clean.

prs.title: fix(core): make file credential store writes atomic and serialized
prs.body:
## Summary

The file-based credential store (`FileKeychain`, used when no native keychain is available) could **silently lose saved credentials** when two processes wrote at the same time. It could also **lock the user out of all saved credentials** if a write was interrupted. This PR makes writes atomic and serializes read-modify-write cycles across processes.

## Details

**Before:**

- `setPassword()` / `deletePassword()` did an unlocked whole-file read-modify-write. With two concurrent writers (e.g. an OAuth token refresh in one terminal and a login in another), both read the same snapshot and the second write erased the first's entry.
- `saveData()` used `fs.writeFile` directly on the live file. A crash or full disk mid-write left a truncated ciphertext. AES-GCM decryption of that always fails, so every later operation threw `Corrupted credentials file detected ...` until the user deleted the file by hand.

**After:**

- **Atomic writes:** `saveData()` writes to a unique `gemini-credentials.json.<uuid>.tmp` (mode `0600`) and `rename`s it over the credentials file. The live file is therefore always a complete old or new version.
  - Transient `EBUSY`/`EPERM` rename failures (Windows, file briefly open elsewhere) are retried with backoff, the same approach as `ProjectRegistry.save()`.
  - The temp file is removed if writing or renaming fails.
- **Cross-process serialization:** `setPassword()` and `deletePassword()` run under an exclusive `proper-lockfile` lock and re-read the file inside the lock.
  - `proper-lockfile` is already a dependency, used by `ProjectRegistry` and trusted folders.
  - `realpath: false` lets the lock be taken before the credentials file exists, so no empty (undecryptable) placeholder file is created.
  - Retries wait up to ~5 s. Stale locks from crashed processes are recovered by `proper-lockfile`'s default stale detection.
- **Reads** (`getPassword`, `findCredentials`) stay lock-free. With atomic renames they always see a complete file.

No change to the file format, encryption, or location.

I did not add a `.bak` self-heal generation, which the issue mentions as optional. With atomic writes, a truncated file can no longer be produced by this code. Happy to add it if maintainers want recovery for files corrupted by older versions.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29054

## How to Validate

```bash
cd packages/core && npx vitest run src/services/fileKeychain.test.ts src/services/gcmTruncationReproduction.test.ts
```

`FileKeychain` had no unit tests. This adds 10, using a real temp directory:

- basic set/get/find/delete, file removal on last delete, encryption at rest, no leftover temp or lock files
- **8 concurrent writers** (separate instances, standing in for separate processes): no entries lost
- **interleaved concurrent set/delete**: no entries dropped or resurrected
- **interrupted write** (partial temp write + `ENOSPC`): the existing file is byte-for-byte unchanged and still decrypts
- the lock is released after a failed write
- transient `EPERM`/`EBUSY` rename is retried; a permanent rename failure cleans up the temp file

The 5 tests covering the bug (both concurrency tests, the interrupted write, and both rename tests) **fail on `main` and pass with this change**.

Note: `keychainService.test.ts` has 5 failures on Windows both on `main` and on this branch. They come from WSL detection in that test's environment, and that test mocks `FileKeychain` entirely, so they are unrelated to this change.

## Summary

Fixes an unhandled promise rejection in `packages/a2a-server/src/agent/task.ts` caused by invoking `this.scheduler.schedule()` with `void`. When tool calls are queued and a task is aborted or cancelled, `CoreToolScheduler` legitimately rejects the promise, triggering an unhandled rejection that terminates the entire `a2a-server` process in Node.js 15+.

## Details

- Attached a targeted `.catch()` handler to `this.scheduler.schedule()` in `scheduleToolCalls`.
- Safely swallows expected abort and cancellation errors (`abortSignal.aborted`, `isAbortError`, and cancellation messages) so that aborting one task does not crash the server or affect other tasks.
- Logs unexpected scheduler errors via `logger.error`.
- Added regression tests in `packages/a2a-server/src/agent/task.test.ts` to ensure cancellation does not emit `unhandledRejection` and unexpected errors are appropriately logged.

Fixes #29034

prs.title: fix(core): stop $ patterns corrupting prompt templates and {{args}}
prs.body:
## Summary

Prompt templates in core were filled with `String.prototype.replace(string, string)`. As a result, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'` and `$$` in model, tool or user text were treated as replacement patterns instead of being inserted as-is. That silently corrupted:

- edit instructions and file contents sent to the LLM edit fixer
- tool output sent to the summarizer
- conversation text sent to the session summarizer

The same problem affected `{{args}}` substitution in custom commands, including inside `!{...}` shell commands. This PR fixes all of these call sites by reusing the existing safe helpers. It adds no new utilities.

## Details

**1. `$` replacement patterns (the reported bug).** For example, `'$&'` in an edit's `old_string` was replaced by the placeholder token itself (`{old_string}`), so the model received a different search string from the one that failed.

**2. Placeholder injection in `llm-edit-fixer` (found while fixing #1).** The five placeholders were filled one after another. Any input that contained a *later* placeholder got substituted into instead of the template. Example: an instruction that mentions `{old_string}`, or code containing `{error}`. That moved user/file content into the wrong section of the prompt.

**Changes:**

- `packages/core/src/utils/llm-edit-fixer.ts`, `packages/core/src/utils/summarizer.ts`, `packages/core/src/services/sessionSummaryService.ts`:
  - Use the existing single-pass `safeTemplateReplace()` from `textUtils.ts`. It is already used by the Conseca policy prompts and already tested for `$&` and double-interpolation.
  - The templates switch from `{key}` to that helper's `{{key}}` placeholder syntax. Each placeholder appears exactly once, so the generated prompts are unchanged for normal input.
- `packages/cli/src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.ts`:
  - All five `replaceAll(SHORTHAND_ARGS_PLACEHOLDER, …)` calls now use the existing `safeLiteralReplace()`.
  - Custom command arguments containing `$` patterns now reach the prompt and the shell command unchanged.
  - The policy check still runs on the final resolved command.

`bugCommand.ts` also uses `.replace('{…}', …)`, but its values go through `encodeURIComponent`, which encodes `$`, so it is not affected and is left as-is.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29044

## How to Validate

```bash
npm run build --workspace @google/gemini-cli-core
cd packages/core && npx vitest run src/utils/llm-edit-fixer.test.ts src/utils/summarizer.test.ts src/services/sessionSummaryService.test.ts src/utils/textUtils.test.ts
cd ../cli && npx vitest run src/services/prompt-processors/shellProcessor.test.ts
```

There are 6 new regression tests: $-patterns in all five edit-fixer inputs, placeholder injection in the edit fixer, $-patterns in summarizer and session-summary input, and $-patterns in raw and shell-escaped `{{args}}`. **All 6 fail on `main` and pass with this change.** The existing prompt-construction tests (including the exact-match summarizer prompt test) pass unchanged.

Manual check: create a custom command with `prompt = "Echo: {{args}}"` and run `/<command> cost is $& or $'`. On `main` the prompt shows `cost is {{args}} or …`. With this change it shows the input exactly.

prs.title: fix(core): prevent path traversal in legacy checkpoint fallback
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes the path-traversal vulnerability in `Logger._getCheckpointPath()` and `Logger.deleteCheckpoint()` when falling back to the legacy unencoded checkpoint filename (`checkpoint-${tag}.json`).

While `_checkpointPath(tag)` safely percent-encodes special characters (including `/` and `\`) via `encodeTagName(tag)`, both `_getCheckpointPath(tag)` and `deleteCheckpoint(tag)` previously fell back to constructing `path.join(this.geminiDir, `checkpoint-${tag}.json`)` directly from the raw `tag`. A tag containing `../` segments (for example, `x/../../target`) caused `path.join` to normalize the `checkpoint-x` prefix away and resolve to `../target.json` outside `this.geminiDir`, allowing `loadCheckpoint`, `checkpointExists`, and `deleteCheckpoint` to read, probe, or delete arbitrary `*.json` files outside the checkpoints directory.

### Key Changes
- **Legacy Path Guard (`packages/core/src/core/logger.ts`)**: Added `_legacyCheckpointPath(tag)` to validate that the legacy candidate filename is a flat basename within `this.geminiDir` with no path separators before `_getCheckpointPath` or `deleteCheckpoint` touches the filesystem.
- **Unit Tests (`packages/core/src/core/logger.test.ts`)**: Added regression coverage verifying that `checkpointExists`, `loadCheckpoint`, and `deleteCheckpoint` reject `../` traversal tags on the legacy fallback path while preserving backward compatibility for flat legacy tags with special characters.

## Related Issues

Closes #29191

## How to Validate

```bash
npx vitest run --root packages/core src/core/logger.test.ts
npx eslint --max-warnings 0 packages/core/src/core/logger.ts packages/core/src/core/logger.test.ts
npm run typecheck --workspace=@google/gemini-cli-core
```
