issues.body:
## Problem

The bundled IMAP trigger already provides useful sender authentication, read-only mailbox access, bounded message fetching, deduplication and contained hook-reader dispatch. I would like to discuss a small, opt-in reliability extension rather than a new email platform.

Some workflows need a durable answer to **“what happened to this mailbox message?”** after a restart. The answer must distinguish:

- source captured or durably referenced;
- agent turn admitted;
- processing completed, failed, skipped or of unknown outcome;
- optional delivery completed, rejected or of unknown outcome.

A successful admission/runId is not evidence of processing completion or delivery.

## Source basis

Reviewed upstream main at **bcb386ad34a89bfa11ac70d8ffe95c6f10929dd8** (2026-10-21). This is source analysis, not a live-provider failure reproduction.

- [IMAP state](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/bcb386ad34a89bfa11ac70d8ffe95c6f10929dd8/extensions/imap/src/state.ts#L18-L101) persists cursor, claims and a bounded Message-ID ring.
- [Watcher processing](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/bcb386ad34a89bfa11ac70d8ffe95c6f10929dd8/extensions/imap/src/watcher.ts#L351-L450) claims a UID before dispatch, releases rejected admission through a bounded retry path, and returns success on accepted admission. The [sweep](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/bcb386ad34a89bfa11ac70d8ffe95c6f10929dd8/extensions/imap/src/watcher.ts#L284-L349) then advances the cursor.
- The [trusted plugin hook contract](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/bcb386ad34a89bfa11ac70d8ffe95c6f10929dd8/src/plugins/runtime/types-core.ts#L462-L479) returns admission success/runId or a rejection reason. The [Gateway facade](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/bcb386ad34a89bfa11ac70d8ffe95c6f10929dd8/src/gateway/server/hooks.ts#L620-L712) does not expose its internal completion promise to the plugin and uses a process-local replay map.
- The [IMAP documentation](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/bcb386ad34a89bfa11ac70d8ffe95c6f10929dd8/docs/automation/imap.md#L156-L171) already documents the admission/crash limitation and that skipped messages are outside the channel ingress dead-letter queue.

Consequently, an admitted turn that later fails is not retried by the watcher; a crash during unresolved admission can leave a deduplication claim. Those are important existing safety tradeoffs, not an exactly-once bug claim.

## Proposed minimum scope

An **optional durable processing handoff** for IMAP, designed around existing host persistence/queue owners:

1. Persist a bounded, immutable event envelope or validated source locator before advancing intake. Bind it to configured mailbox identity, UIDVALIDITY and UID; retain Message-ID as metadata, not the sole identity.
2. Retain an inspectable lifecycle record linking that identity to admission and terminal processing facts. Where delivery is involved, keep execution and delivery outcomes distinct.
3. Recover pending work across restart only when ownership and prior execution state are known. Preserve an explicit held/unknown state for unresolved admission or sends; do not blindly rerun an admitted model turn or resend after an uncertain ACK.
4. Make failed/skipped/held entries discoverable with bounded retention and secret-free reason codes. Any future operator resubmission should be explicit and must not reset a mailbox cursor or discard delivered receipts.
5. Preserve today's default behavior unless the durable mode is explicitly enabled. Define fresh-install and UIDVALIDITY-reset policy rather than implicitly replaying a mailbox.

The exact API shape is open. If a supported existing queue/outcome API can provide these guarantees, documentation and a thin IMAP adapter may be sufficient.

## Reuse existing infrastructure

OpenClaw already has [plugin state/blob/ingress queue APIs](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/bcb386ad34a89bfa11ac70d8ffe95c6f10929dd8/src/plugins/runtime/types-core.ts#L567-L609), an [ingress lifecycle contract](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/bcb386ad34a89bfa11ac70d8ffe95c6f10929dd8/src/channels/message/ingress-queue.types.ts#L157-L246), and [outbound unknown-send reconciliation](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/bcb386ad34a89bfa11ac70d8ffe95c6f10929dd8/src/infra/outbound/delivery-queue-recovery.ts#L559-L643). This proposal should reuse those owners, not introduce a parallel queue or retry framework.

Direct HTTP hooks can wait for completion, but an in-process completion promise or a single HTTP response alone does not provide restart-persistent custody. A small trusted outcome lookup/event seam may be needed; whether it belongs in the SDK or remains IMAP-local needs maintainer guidance.

## Non-goals

- Exactly-once processing/delivery guarantees.
- A new SMTP sender, provider migration or general task orchestration framework.
- Application-specific sender lists, task identifiers, routing/fallback policies, notification schedules or agent roles.
- Automatic execution of attachments or instructions inside mail.
- Treating extraction availability or agent completion as proof a human/model understood every part.
- Automatic Seen mutation; read-only mailbox behavior should remain unchanged.
- Weakening sender authentication, plugin trust, containment or tool policy.

Full-original/attachment retrieval could be a separate extension. The minimum handoff must describe truncation and source availability honestly; it need not ship an OCR/document-processing pipeline.

## Related work / duplicate boundary

- [#137871](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/137871) and [PR #138120](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/138120): explicit IMAP delivery targets. This discussion is **not** another channel/to request.
- [#173952](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/173952) and [PR #176606](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/176606): execution status versus canceled delivery.
- [#7281](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/7281): generic hook fallback; outside the minimum scope here.
- The official [AgentMail plugin's durable receive adapter](https://github.com/agentmail-to/openclaw-plugin/blob/4ae26ff564d59ad9f81e897ca5c9da940ba58d0e/src/channel/src/durable-receive.ts#L150-L210) demonstrates useful reuse of host ingress queues for a different provider. It is an architectural analogue, not IMAP checkpoint compatibility.

## Suggested synthetic acceptance cases

Use a loopback fake mailbox/reader/transport, isolated temporary state and no production credentials:

- Crash before/after persisted handoff, admission acknowledgement and cursor advancement.
- Processing failure after admission; restart before terminal-outcome persistence.
- Repeated same-UID intake, Message-ID collision and UIDVALIDITY change.
- Lost send ACK and restart with an already-started platform send.
- Capacity/retention exhaustion: no eviction of admitted pending work or advancement past unretained input.
- Safe opt-in migration from existing cursor state without mailbox replay or silent baseline gaps.

Every case should identify the retained owner, stage and outcome; “unknown” is valid when it is honest and does not cause blind replay.

## Questions for maintainers

1. Is durable IMAP handoff a suitable bundled-plugin extension, or is an existing supported ingress/outcome composition preferred?
2. Is there already a restart-persistent trusted-hook outcome interface this should consume?
3. What is the smallest acceptable operator inspection/recovery surface?

I would like to settle scope and ownership in discussion before proposing implementation.

## Alternatives considered

Keep an external IMAP consumer with its own ledger (works, but duplicates transport and authentication ownership); compose HTTP hooks with waitForCompletion (still requires restart-persistent custody); use AgentMail (different provider, not an IMAP checkpoint migration). Prefer a thin supported composition of existing native queue/outcome primitives where possible.

## Impact

Affected: operators using bundled IMAP for asynchronous agent workflows that need per-message recovery and auditability. This is a reliability/recovery gap around crashes or admitted processing failures, not a claim of routine loss. Consequence: operators must reconstruct outcomes from logs and original mail or maintain a separate lifecycle ledger. No production incident rate is claimed; evidence here is source analysis.

## Implementation intent

Maybe, with maintainer guidance. We plan to review discussion in approximately two weeks before deciding whether to propose a narrowly scoped PR.

issues.body:
## Summary

Allow automatic audio transcript echo to be disabled for a specific Telegram group or topic while preserving internal transcription and `requireMention: false`.

## Problem to solve

I have a Telegram group where the agent is intentionally allowed to read and respond without a direct mention. It should continue understanding voice notes, but it should not publish a transcript of every voice note into the group.

The global `tools.media.audio.echoTranscript` switch cannot express this: turning it off also removes transcript echoes from unrelated conversations. Telegram group/topic settings currently have no separate echo override.

This is distinct from admission-based echo suppression. When `requireMention: false`, an unmentioned message can legitimately pass admission. Passing admission should not force a public transcription receipt.

## Proposed solution

Add a Telegram group-level transcript echo override, with topic-level inheritance and overrides. For example, the following is proposed syntax, not a currently supported setting:

- `channels.telegram.groups.<chatId>.echoTranscript: false`
- `channels.telegram.groups.<chatId>.topics.<threadId>.echoTranscript: false`

An omitted setting should preserve existing behavior. A topic should inherit its group's effective echo policy unless explicitly overridden. The setting must control only automatic transcript publication, not STT, model-facing transcript availability, message admission, or ordinary agent replies.

A future `direct-address-only` echo policy would also be useful, but it is not required for this request. It would need an independent addressing decision rather than treating admission as a mention.

### Acceptance criteria

- With audio understanding and global echo enabled, a group with `requireMention: false` and echo disabled still transcribes and processes ambient voice notes, without posting automatic transcript echoes.
- Mentioned messages and replies to the bot still reach the normal agent pipeline. Under the proposed `false` override, they also produce no automatic echo.
- Existing DM and unrelated-group echo behavior is unchanged.
- Topic inheritance and explicit overrides are covered by tests.
- Both preflight and normal media-understanding echo paths respect the effective policy, without suppressing the internal transcript.
- If a direct-address-only policy is implemented later, test ambient, explicit-mention, and reply-to-bot cases separately from admission.

## Alternatives considered

- Global echo off affects other chats.
- `requireMention: true` changes the intended ambient-agent behavior.
- Disabling audio understanding or denying its scope loses voice-note context.
- `disableAudioPreflight` only changes preflight mention checking.
- A system prompt cannot reliably control the automatic echo sent before agent processing.

## Impact

Affected: Telegram groups using ambient agents with audio understanding and transcript echo enabled elsewhere.

Severity: disruptive channel noise, not lost transcription. It occurs for each successfully transcribed voice note that produces an enabled echo.

## Evidence/examples

Reviewed stock `v2026.10.5` and main `690e0dd0b8fbc1ced8ddfe1e9d08fc302831e023` on 2026-10-21. This is source-based configuration research, not an exact-version live reproduction.

Related work:
- #146348 defers preflight echo until admission, but does not add an independent echo policy for admitted, unmentioned messages.
- #142829 adds local-Whisper echo/backend filtering.
- #162565 addresses same-source replay duplication.
- #166640 addresses quoted-audio re-echo.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this if it remains unimplemented after one month.

issues.body:
## Summary

When a `before_agent_run` hook blocks a run, any message that was **steered** into that run while it was being prepared is never committed to the transcript. The queue then waits the full `DEFAULT_QUEUE_TRANSCRIPT_COMMIT_TIMEOUT_MS` (120 s) for it. Until that timer runs out, the block reply is held back and later messages in the same session queue behind it.

Version: `openclaw@2026.7.1-2`, Telegram channel, `dmScope: "per-peer"`.

## Why it matters

`before_agent_run` is the natural place to enforce a policy on every channel, and a block is the expected outcome there, not an error. We use it in [Pinchy](https://github.com/heypinchy/pinchy) to enforce monthly cost budgets (heypinchy/pinchy#1228): when an agent's budget is used up, the plugin returns `{ outcome: "block", reason: "budget_exhausted", message }`, and the sender should get "Your message could not be sent: …" right away.

A user who gets no answer tends to send a second message ("hello?"). If that second message lands while the first run is still being prepared, it is steered into that run, and the refusal then shows up two minutes late. The block itself still works; the delay makes the agent look broken rather than paused.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Register a plugin with `before_agent_run` that returns `{ outcome: "block", reason: "test", message: "blocked" }`. Set `plugins.entries.<id>.hooks.allowConversationAccess: true`.
2. Send a Telegram DM to the agent, then send a second DM within the short window before the hook has answered. Slowing the hook down by about 1 s makes the window easy to hit.
3. Observe:
   - **Expected:** both messages are refused at once, each with the block reply.
   - **Actual:** the gateway log shows `before_agent_run hook blocked by <plugin>` immediately, but the refusal reaches Telegram only about 120 s later. Messages sent in between wait behind it.

## Where it seems to come from

In `dist/selection-*.js`, `steerActiveSessionWithOptionalDeliveryWait` calls `steerAndWaitForTranscriptCommit(activeSession, text, options.deliveryTimeoutMs ?? DEFAULT_QUEUE_TRANSCRIPT_COMMIT_TIMEOUT_MS, …)`, which resolves only on the queued user message's end event (`isQueuedUserMessageEnd`). When the active run is blocked before model input, the steered message never produces that event, so the wait runs out instead of resolving.

## Possible fix

When a run ends with a `before_agent_run` block, settle any steered messages that are waiting on its transcript commit right away. Either run each one through the gate as its own turn, or refuse it with the same block decision. Either way the queue would not have to wait out the timeout.

Related, but a different question: #78830 (a `before_steering` hook).

**Version:** OpenClaw 2026.10.5 (1b58cb9)

## What happened
After a recovery that moved the old session store aside, `openclaw doctor` stops at:

```
Failing check transcript-directives (step-refused): Skipped historical transcript directive migration:
OpenClawAgentDatabaseLeaseActiveError: Agent main database is still open in another process;
stop that process and rerun openclaw doctor --fix.
Failing check migration-detection / device-auth / device-identity / meeting-transcripts (blocked-by-prior-refusal)
```

The only holder of the agent DB is the running gateway itself.


## Steps to reproduce
Deterministic on our host:
1. Run OpenClaw 2026.10.5 as a systemd user service (gateway running).
2. Have a pending historical transcript directive migration. Ours came after the session store was moved aside and the gateway started on a fresh agent DB; `openclaw doctor` reports `[plugin_migration_source_retained] ... remain pending for plugin(s): discord`.
3. With the gateway still running, run `openclaw doctor --fix`.

**Expected:** the migration completes online, or doctor offers an online path.
**Actual:** `transcript-directives` is refused with `OpenClawAgentDatabaseLeaseActiveError`. `migration-detection`, `device-auth`, `device-identity` and `meeting-transcripts` are then skipped as `blocked-by-prior-refusal`. The only process holding the agent DB is the gateway, which `pgrep` + `/proc/<pid>/fd` confirm is a single holder.

## Impact
- Running the repair needs a gateway stop. For an always-on gateway, every repair means downtime.
- Until it runs, the half-migrated store degrades live features: `cron runs` returns "Automation not found" for job ids that `cron list` just returned, and tool calls intermittently fail with "Direct shared-state reader requires current integrity admission".
- One refused step blocks four unrelated later steps.

## Asks
1. Let the running gateway perform this migration itself (it already holds the lease), or offer `doctor --fix --online`.
2. Don't block independent later steps on an unrelated refusal.
3. Make the error say that the lease holder is the gateway and that stopping it is required.

## Related
#164948 (doctor self-deadlock on state sqlite), #151363

issues.body:
## Background

The `extensions/a2a` channel plugin currently implements only a partial, 0.3-era subset of the A2A protocol. The A2A protocol has since shipped **v1.0** (new method surface, HTTP+JSON/REST binding, revised error model and HTTP status mappings, extended agent card, required-extension negotiation, push notification config CRUD, card caching semantics), and the official conformance suite [a2a-tck](https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-tck) is now available to verify implementations against it.

## What was done

I have implemented **full A2A protocol v1.0 conformance** for the a2a plugin, and validated it against the official a2a-tck conformance suite:

- **All 11 v1.0 JSON-RPC methods**, plus backward-compatible 0.3-era dotted aliases so existing clients keep working
- **HTTP+JSON (REST) binding** at `/a2a/v1/rest` (spec §5.4) with gRPC-transcoding-style path bindings
- **SSE streaming** with resumable task updates
- **Full v1.0 error model**: codes `-32001..-32009` with `google.rpc.ErrorInfo` details, and the spec-mandated HTTP status mappings (409 / 415 / 502)
- **Agent Card caching** (ETag / Last-Modified / Cache-Control / 304) at `/.well-known/agent-card.json`, plus the **Extended Agent Card** behind the `extendedAgentCard` capability
- **Push notification config CRUD** with idempotent delete, webhook delivery with SSRF protection, and configurable auth schemes
- **Capability, media-type, and required-extension validation** (spec §3.3.4, §3.1.1, §4.6)

## a2a-tck results

- Latest round: **~73% overall / ~74% of MUST requirements passing**
- All P0/P1 findings from earlier rounds are fixed and confirmed passing
- The only remaining failures are `DM-ART-001` / `DM-MSG-001`, which by design require a scripted reference SUT that echoes `tck-artifact-*` prefixes — not applicable to an LLM-backed gateway

## Configuration compatibility

All pre-existing config keys keep their names, semantics, and defaults — the upgrade is **fully backward compatible**. New v1.0 features (capabilities, push notifications, REST binding, extended card) are opt-in via new keys. `src/config/bundled-channel-config-metadata.generated.ts` is regenerated so core startup validation accepts the new keys.

## Implementation

Tracked in PR #179380. Feedback from maintainers on scope, structure, or config naming is very welcome.

issues.body:
src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/provider-prompt-state.ts computes the provider prompt snapshot in two steps:

- :133 - providerPromptWorkerBytes(params.payload) walks the payload on the calling thread to estimate the byte size.
  The walk returns undefined for any member that is a Proxy or that has a toJSON method (:79-81), and also for
  function/symbol/bigint values (:74-76).
- :135-146 - if the estimate is a number, the real work runs in the shared compute worker pool (:137). Otherwise the
  whole snapshot is prepared inline on the calling thread (:146), and the same inline path is used when the worker
  fails (:144).

The inline path is not logged and not counted, so a session that regularly hits it looks completely normal while the
Gateway event loop does the JSON serialization and the SHA-256 hashing of the full request body.

Measured with the function extracted verbatim from the tree, on a 1.6 MB payload:

- JSON.stringify of the request body: 2.79 ms
- sha256 over the serialized bytes: 1.96 ms
- total event-loop time per provider request: ~4.8 ms

Any single Date (or SDK object exposing toJSON) anywhere in the payload is enough to select this path - the failure
mode is a property of one nested member, not of the payload size.

Note: the cost of the size walk itself is small and node-counting rather than byte-scanning (0.09-0.64 ms for payloads
from 100 KB to 128 MB), so the problem here is not the walk - it is the silent switch to inline execution.

Proposal:

- log at debug level (or count in a metric) when the inline path is taken and why (unmeasurable payload vs worker failure),
- and/or move the inline path into the same worker by passing the payload without the toJSON guard, so the fallback
  keeps the same execution model.

Duplicate check: no upstream issue or PR found for this fallback. The nearest change is #159574 (merged 2026-09-27),
which removed the second traversal of large model requests, and #179142 (open PR) reuses the wire JSON for provider
prompt fingerprints; neither covers the inline fallback selected by the toJSON guard.

Verification: read src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/provider-prompt-state.ts lines 69-113 (the guard) and 133-146 (the
branching), and time prepareProviderPrompt on a 1.6 MB payload with and without a Date member in the payload.

Version: openclaw 2026.7.1-2 (memory-core plugin; dist refs: `dreaming-Cth0w6SG.js`, `dreaming-DqzMSXGC.js`, `dreaming-phases-DCJr5DsV.js`, `short-term-promotion-stx0l04M.js`)

## 1. `dreaming.phases.deep.limit=0` disables the entire unified sweep (light + REM too)

The unified dreaming cron gate is computed as:

```js
// dreaming-DqzMSXGC.js
enabled: resolved.enabled && resolved.phases.deep.enabled
```

So `phases.deep.enabled=false` makes the reconciler remove the single managed dreaming cron job — light and REM die with deep, because all three phases share one job and their own `enabled` bits are only read inside the job payload (`runDreamingSweepPhases`).

The intuitive workaround — keep `deep.enabled=true` and set `phases.deep.limit=0` to suppress only auto-promotion — does **not** work, because the `limit === 0` check is a global early return placed **before** the sweep, not a promotion-scoped gate:

```js
// dreaming-Cth0w6SG.js — runShortTermDreamingPromotionIfTriggered
if (params.config.limit === 0) {
    params.logger.info("memory-core: dreaming promotion skipped because limit=0.");
    return { handled: true, reason: "memory-core: short-term dreaming disabled by limit" }; // <- sweep never reached
}
// ...only after this: runDreamingSweepPhases(...) → rank → apply
```

**Expected:** `limit` should gate only the promotion step (rank/apply), or light/REM sweep should be triggerable independently of the deep-phase gate. Right now there is no first-class config for "keep collecting light/REM candidates, never auto-promote".

**Current workaround** (shipped in production): `deep.enabled=true` + `deep.minRecallCount=999999`, exploiting the hard filter `signalCount < minRecallCount → continue` (`short-term-promotion-stx0l04M.js:1558`, re-checked in apply at `:1897`). This restores the sweep while forcing Ranked 0 / Promoted 0 — but it's a magic number, a proper switch would be better.

## 2. `dreaming.phases.deep.recovery.*` is parsed but never consumed (dead config)

`resolveMemoryDreamingConfig()` resolves the full `deep.recovery` subtree (`enabled`, `triggerBelowHealth`, `lookbackDays`, `maxRecoveredCandidates`, `minRecoveryConfidence`, `autoWriteMinConfidence`) in `dreaming-DqzMSXGC.js`, but no other dist module references these keys (verified by grep across all shipped dist bundles; the only hits are the resolver itself and unrelated modules' own "recovery" strings).

Config authors can reasonably believe they're configuring a recovery auto-write path (e.g. `autoWriteMinConfidence` sounds like it can write MEMORY.md) while it does nothing. Either wire it up or drop it from the resolver/schema.

Happy to split into two issues if that helps triage.

issues.body:
# Subagent-Abschluss: State-Event-Buchung und Registry-Persistenz schlagen fehl

**Kurzfassung:** Bei Subagenten-Abschluessen schlagen zwei Buchungspfade fehl: die State-Event-Buchung (`Subagent terminal signal owner changed before commit`) und die Persistenz der Subagent-Registry (`Queued subagent registry persistence failed`). Im Funktionstest mit Run 13cf69c7-c4ef-4044-bc68-12385a07562b wurde das Ergebnis beim Parent bestaetigt. Fuer die uebrigen Faelle wurde die Ergebniszustellung nicht vollstaendig geprueft; Ergebnisverlust ist weder belegt noch ausgeschlossen. Unvollstaendig sind Timeline/State-Event und teilweise der `subagent_ended`-Hook. Im 14-Tage-Fenster: 38 State-Event-Fehler, 6 Hook-Fehler, davon nur 3 Runs mit beiden Fehlern. Die beiden Meldungsfamilien werden daher getrennt gefuehrt.

## 1. Umgebung

- OpenClaw 2026.9.7 (Build c074824)
- Node v24.19.0
- Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, Kernel 7.0.0-15-generic, x86_64
- Gateway als systemd-User-Unit, 15 Agenten, davon 274 Subagenten-Sessions
- Cross-Agent-Konfiguration aktiv: main-orchestrator mit subagents.allowAgents auf vier Ziel-Agenten
- Datenquelle: journalctl --user -u openclaw-gateway.service, Fenster 14 Tage (07.10. bis 21.10.2026)

## 2. Beobachtungen (belegt)

### 2.1 State-Event-Buchung schlaegt fehl

Meldung:
```
[sessions/state-events] failed to record session state event:
  Error: Subagent terminal signal owner changed before commit
```

- 38 Vorkommen in 14 Tagen
- Verteilung: 17.10.: 1 | 18.10.: 3 | 19.10.: 23 | 20.10.: 9 | 21.10.: 2
- Zeitliche Zuordnung: 35 von 38 liegen innerhalb von +/-3 s zu genau EINER Zeile 'run <id> ended with stopReason=stop' (0 mehrdeutig, 3 ohne Zuordnung)
- Beobachtet bei Cross-Agent-Spawns (Parent-Agent ungleich Kind-Agent)

### 2.2 Hook-Emission schlaegt fehl (eigener Fehler, abweichender gemeldeter Fehlergrund)

Meldung:
```
[agents/subagent-registry-completion] failed to emit subagent_ended hook for run <id>:
  Queued subagent registry persistence failed: ...
```

- 6 Vorkommen in 14 Tagen
- Betroffene Runs: 71d21603-e2db-47ee-b3b8-c2d24fe3dbae, 1bb2d815-0684-49ff-8859-46259233f993,
  4cfd6c89-1a92-47d7-953a-6866da1b1a97, e01f6385-dfc3-4e15-8a5e-f9992a72ce5a,
  ce0777bf-dded-4eb5-86d5-f3f187e90e6c, 2ab4b8b5-9095-4942-a864-cfb1141f254a
- Die Meldung nennt als Grund die Persistenz der Subagent-Registry (Queued), NICHT einen Owner-Wechsel

### 2.3 Ueberschneidung — bewusst restriktiv ausgewiesen

- Nur **3 Runs** zeigen beide Fehler eindeutig:
  - 1bb2d815-0684-49ff-8859-46259233f993
  - 2ab4b8b5-9095-4942-a864-cfb1141f254a
  - ce0777bf-dded-4eb5-86d5-f3f187e90e6c
- **3 Hook-Fehler ohne zugeordneten State-Fehler**: 71d21603..., 4cfd6c89..., e01f6385...
- **32 zugeordnete State-Fehler ohne Hook-Fehler**; drei weitere State-Fehler bleiben ohne Run-Zuordnung.
- Folge: Die beiden Meldungsfamilien duerfen NICHT als ein Fehlerfall gefuehrt werden. Sie ueberlappen nur in 3 von 38 bzw. 3 von 6 Faellen. Eine gemeinsame Ursache ist damit weder belegt noch ausgeschlossen.

### 2.4 Sanitisierte Logauszuege (Host, IP und Pfade maskiert; Run-IDs erhalten)

```
# Run mit BEIDEN Fehlern (Beispiel 1bb2d815...)
2026-10-18T08:43:04.498+00:00 [agents/agent-command] run 1bb2d815-0684-49ff-8859-46259233f993 ended with stopReason=stop
2026-10-18T08:43:04.562+00:00 [sessions/state-events] failed to record session state event: Error: Subagent terminal signal owner changed before commit
2026-10-18T08:43:39.441+00:00 [agents/subagent-registry-completion] failed to emit subagent_ended hook for run 1bb2d815-...: Queued subagent registry persistence failed

# Run mit BEIDEN Fehlern (2ab4b8b5...)
2026-10-20T18:31:54.211+00:00 [agents/agent-command] run 2ab4b8b5-9095-4942-a864-cfb1141f254a ended with stopReason=stop
2026-10-20T18:31:54.326+00:00 [sessions/state-events] failed to record session state event: Error: Subagent terminal signal owner changed before commit
2026-10-20T18:31:54.543+00:00 [agents/subagent-registry-completion] failed to emit subagent_ended hook for run 2ab4b8b5-...: Queued subagent registry persistence failed

# Run NUR mit State-Fehler (13cf69c7...), Abschluss kam beim Parent an
2026-10-21T08:11:25.207+00:00 [agents/agent-command] run 13cf69c7-c4ef-4044-bc68-12385a07562b ended with stopReason=stop
2026-10-21T08:11:25.318+00:00 [sessions/state-events] failed to record session state event: Error: Subagent terminal signal owner changed before commit
```

## 3. Hypothesen (nicht bestaetigt)

- **H1 (State-Event):** Der Terminal-Schreiber prueft vor dem Commit `isCurrentSessionEffectsOwner() && hasCurrentTerminalOutcome()`. Bei Cross-Agent-Spawns wechselt die Effects-Ownership waehrend des Laufs; die Pruefung schlaegt fehl und die Buchung wird verworfen. Unklar: ob der Wechsel regelkonform ist oder ein Timing-Effekt.
- **H2 (Hook):** Die Registry-Persistenz laeuft ueber eine Queue; unter SQLite-Schreiblast schlaegt der Queue-Commit fehl. In der Naehe der Fehler stehen gelegentlich '[session-sqlite] slow SQLite reclamation'-Zeilen. Unklar: welcher Constraint verletzt wird.
- **H3 (gemeinsame Ursache):** Bislang weder belegt noch ausgeschlossen. Die unterschiedlichen Fehlertexte und nur 3 gemeinsame Runs sprechen gegen eine einfache gemeinsame Ursache, schliessen sie aber nicht aus.

## 4. Code-Stellen

```js
// dist/subagent-registry-Dtv0qGd_.mjs:2349 (identisch in package-update-activation-recovery.mjs:1493376)
if (!isCurrentSessionEffectsOwner() || !hasCurrentTerminalOutcome())
  throw new Error("Subagent terminal signal owner changed before commit");

// dist/subagent-registry-state-B6QeHDwp.mjs:79
super(`Queued subagent registry persistence failed: ${formatErrorMessage(cause)}`, { cause: failure });

// verwandte Waechter
// dist/agent-run-terminal-writes-CFOeBDjV.mjs:39  -> Terminal write owner changed before commit
// dist/main-session-restart-recovery-marking-C8XYS4Nf.mjs:148 -> Restart recovery owner changed before commit
// dist/package-update-activation-recovery.mjs:625506 -> Subagent abort-marker owner changed before commit
```

## 5. Beobachteter Testablauf / Reproduktionsversuch

1. Zwei Agenten mit unterschiedlicher agentId konfigurieren; der Spawner hat subagents.allowAgents fuer das Ziel.
2. Spawner startet einen Subagenten mit trivialem Auftrag (Antwort: OK).
3. Beim Abschluss wurde in einem Fall der State-Event-Fehler beobachtet (2026-10-21T08:11:25.318Z, Run 13cf69c7-c4ef-4044-bc68-12385a07562b), ohne Hook-Fehler. Ob der Fehler bei Wiederholung reproduzierbar ist, ist offen.
4. Fuer den Hook-Fehler wurden mehrere Subagenten unter SQLite-Schreiblast kurz hintereinander abgeschlossen; dabei traten 6 Beobachtungen auf. Ob die Lastabhaengigkeit ursaechlich ist und ob der Fehler reproduzierbar ist, ist offen.

Wiederholbarkeit und Lastabhaengigkeit sind damit nicht belegt.

## 6. Erwartet versus beobachtet

| | Erwartet | Beobachtet |
|---|---|---|
| Abschluss-Signal | State-Event gebucht, Hook emittiert | Buchung fehlt, Hook teils fehlend; Parent-Zustellung nur im Funktionstest 13cf69c7… bestaetigt |
| Ergebnis | vollstaendig | im Funktionstest 13cf69c7… beim Parent bestaetigt; fuer die uebrigen Faelle nicht vollstaendig geprueft (Ergebnisverlust weder belegt noch ausgeschlossen) |
| Timeline/Katalog | vollstaendig | unvollstaendig |

## 7. Was dieses Issue NICHT behauptet

- Kein belegter Datenverlust am fachlichen Ergebnis. Im Funktionstest 13cf69c7… wurde das Ergebnis beim Parent bestaetigt; fuer die uebrigen Faelle wurde die Ergebniszustellung nicht vollstaendig geprueft — Ergebnisverlust ist weder belegt noch ausgeschlossen.
- Eine gemeinsame Ursache ist bislang weder belegt noch ausgeschlossen (nur 3 ueberlappende Runs).
- Keine Aussage ueber andere Versionen oder Builds.

issues.body:
### Summary

A pre-upgrade personalized impact report: match the local installation's manifest (agents, channels, cron jobs, plugins, skills, config keys actually in use) against the target release's changelog, deprecations, and removals, and print "which of *your* configured surfaces this upgrade touches" before anything is swapped.

### Problem to solve

Releases are large (2026.10.5 alone spans ~2,700 commits / ~2,250 PRs) and upgrades are the single loudest source of user pain: recurring reports of cron jobs, channel bindings, and config shapes breaking across a version bump, discovered only after cutover when the daily report doesn't arrive. A user with 5 agents, 3 channels, and a dozen schedules cannot triage a release notes page of that size against their own install, so the rational choices become "never upgrade" or "upgrade and pray".

Post-upgrade monitoring (#159743) and versioned upgrade recipes (#164433) attack the problem after and during cutover. What is missing is the **decision aid before cutover**: a read-only, offline answer to "given what I actually run, what does this release change for me, and what should I check or migrate first?"

### Proposed solution

1. Build (and reuse) a redacted **installation manifest**: enabled channels, agents and their runtimes/models, cron jobs and their schedules, plugins, skills, auth profile kinds, and the set of config keys with non-default values. Much of this overlaps with the baseline manifest already proposed in #159743 — the same primitive serves both.
2. Ship machine-readable **release metadata** per version: touched subsystems (the labels/changelog already encode app areas), config keys added/renamed/removed/deprecated, schema migrations, and behavior changes tagged by surface (cron, channels.*, providers, sandbox, UI).
3. `openclaw update --plan <target>` (or a doctor subcommand): diff the manifest against the target's metadata and print a grouped report — "you use `channels.telegram.*`: 3 changes, 1 deprecation, migration required for X; your cron jobs are unaffected; plugin Y needs a new permission grant".
4. Read-only by design: no downloads, no mutation; safe to run before deciding.

### Alternatives considered

- Reading changelogs manually: does not scale to release size; deprecations affecting *your* keys are invisible in a flat list.
- Post-upgrade survey alone (#159743): catches regressions after damage; a pre-flight diff prevents the avoidable subset.
- Locking versions forever: the failure mode the update contract ("updates always work") exists to eliminate.

### Impact

- Affected: every self-hosting operator, hardest on small-op / single-admin installs without staging environments.
- Severity: upgrade avoidance or multi-day breakage recovery.
- Frequency: every release cycle (multiple per month).
- Consequence: broken schedules and bindings discovered late, manual forensics, eroded trust in updating.

### Evidence/examples

- Recurring "update failure" issue wave each release (e.g. #178976, #178177) and repeated community reports of cron/channel breakage across version bumps.
- Complementary primitives already proposed: #159743 (post-upgrade survey + baseline manifest), #164433 (versioned upgrade recipes), #178016 (`config diff` between disk and effective config — the manifest piece is a natural sibling).

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, proposing the idea only

### Additional information

Scope note: this is intentionally the *planning/reporting* slice, not another updater. If maintainers prefer, the manifest piece could be extracted and shared with #159743 rather than built twice.

issues.body:
### Summary

An opt-in usage budget contract: per-surface (agent / channel / cron job / subagent) token-cost rollups plus a simple enforceable budget hook that can degrade the model, pause a non-critical schedule, or stop the turn when a configured window is exhausted.

### Problem to solve

Cost attribution and cost *control* are currently two different gaps:

- Attribution is fragmented: #102807 shows usage is provider-keyed rather than credential-keyed so mixed API+subscription installs display the wrong billing mode; #90911 notes per-run token accounting exists on `cron_run_logs` but not on `task_runs`/`subagent_runs`; #156999 shows legacy cron sessions land in an "Unattributed" bucket. Operators cannot answer "which of my automations burned the budget".
- Control is essentially absent: a runaway loop, a session-reset re-seeding storm (see #178953), or a chatty channel can consume a full 5-hour plan window in minutes with nothing in the product to stop or downgrade it. Users discover this only at the provider's rate-limit wall.

With recurring autonomous schedules (cron, heartbeats, subagents) being a core deployment pattern, spend needs to be attributable per surface and bounded per policy, the same way tool execution is gated per turn.

### Proposed solution

1. **Attribution rollup contract**: every model call carries the originating surface (agent, channel, cron job id, subagent run, interactive session) end-to-end, and a single queryable aggregate exposes tokens/cost grouped by surface over a time window. This generalizes the parity ask in #90911 and fixes the bucket problems in #102807/#156999 at the data model layer rather than per-UI-widget.
2. **Opt-in budget hook**: a config-scoped budget (per surface or global, per rolling window). On exhaustion the configured action fires: degrade to a cheaper model, skip/pause a schedule with a recorded reason, or fail the turn with a user-visible error — never a silent continue.
3. **Decision-friendly enforcement point**: the budget check belongs at the owning boundary where the next model call is admitted. The recently introduced provider-neutral `decision_evaluate` capability (#155115) is a natural fit for the "what do I do at the limit" judgment, keeping the mechanism generic and opt-in.

Explicitly **not** proposed: a billing system, per-token pricing tables, or provider-specific quota mirroring beyond what exists today.

### Alternatives considered

- Per-provider usage display fixes alone (e.g. #169428's footer template): treats symptoms; no enforcement.
- External monitoring scripts watching usage files: exactly the out-of-tree watcher pattern the project keeps absorbing back into core (cf. #161049 for cron supervision).

### Impact

- Affected: every operator running unattended schedules or multi-agent setups; mixed API+subscription users.
- Severity: cost surprises at "uninstalled it" magnitude are reported; for subscribed plans, wasted 5h windows block real work.
- Frequency: continuous for automation-heavy installs.
- Consequence: unpredictable spend, rate-limit lockouts, and manual post-hoc forensics across session files.

### Evidence/examples

- #90911 (per-run token persistence parity), #102807 (provider-keyed attribution), #156999 (unattributed cron sessions), #7379 (usage footer ask).
- Session-reset re-seeding as a concrete unbounded amplifier: #178953.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, proposing the idea only

### Additional information

If the attribution layer lands first (it is independently useful), the budget hook could follow as a small policy gate; happy to split this into two requests if maintainers prefer.

issues.body:
### Summary

Surface native CLI session reset/drift telemetry (reason, count, affected agent, and re-seeding token overhead) in `status`/`doctor` output and logs, so operators can see when and why an agent is losing its live session context instead of only noticing degraded behavior.

### Problem to solve

OpenClaw invalidates and re-seeds native runtime sessions (claude-cli, codex, etc.) whenever the prompt-prefix identity drifts (`resolveCliSessionReuse` in `src/agents/cli-session.ts`, reasons such as `prompt-tools` / `system-prompt`). Today this is近乎 invisible:

- #178953 reports an install going from 0 to **32 `reason=prompt-tools` resets per day** after an update, discovered only by grepping gateway logs; the user-visible symptom was just "the agent loses most of its working context, often mid-task".
- #178982 and the broader session/context family (the largest issue cluster in the tracker) show the same pattern: users experience the agent "getting dumber" with no way to tell that sessions are being recycled under them.

Each reset also re-seeds the session from saved history, which invalidates prompt-prefix caching and re-sends the full context — a direct token/cost amplifier that is currently unmeasurable from the outside.

### Proposed solution

1. Persist a bounded ring of session-reset events per agent: timestamp, runtime, drift reason, old/new session ids, and trigger context (e.g. "tool set changed on subagent-completion turn").
2. Expose an aggregate in `openclaw status` / `doctor`: resets per agent in the last 24h/7d, grouped by reason.
3. Log a structured, greppable event at reset time (the raw log line exists today, but there is no aggregated view).
4. Optionally report the approximate token overhead caused by re-seeding (bytes re-sent for the rebuilt prefix), so the cost of instability is visible next to usage numbers.

This is deliberately an observability contract, not a behavior change: it makes an existing silent failure mode measurable, per the project principle that every action should have a visible outcome or a recorded intentional non-outcome.

### Alternatives considered

- Fixing each reset trigger individually (e.g. #178953's capability-dependent tool hash). Necessary, but triggers keep evolving; without telemetry the next regression is discovered the same painful way.
- Relying on debug logs. Requires knowing what to grep for after the fact; not actionable for operators.

### Impact

- Affected: any deployment using native CLI runtimes (claude-cli, codex) — multi-agent and subagent-heavy setups most.
- Severity: blocks reliable long-horizon work (context loss mid-task).
- Frequency: continuous on affected installs (dozens of resets/day reported).
- Consequence: silent quality degradation, duplicated messages, and unexplained token spend.

### Evidence/examples

- #178953 — 0 → 32 `reason=prompt-tools` resets/day, user-invisible until log grep.
- #178982 — `claude-cli` sessions reset on `reason=prompt-tools` for tool-catalog drift.
- Session/context management is the largest open-issue theme in the tracker over the last month (~35 new issues).

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

### Additional information

Related but narrower: #164972 asks for test-matrix visibility for claude-cli teams; this request is about runtime reset telemetry for operators.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Summary

In a browser Talk session, each `talk-realtime-consult-*` run makes the next consult's provider history differ from the previous request at the previous consult's prompt. On Anthropic the cache read falls back to the system prompt on almost every consult, so each spoken question re-writes the whole conversation into the prompt cache.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Agent on `anthropic/claude-opus-5-5` (5-minute cache) with a long-running session.
2. Open a browser Talk session and ask two questions that both trigger an agent consult, 30–90 s apart.
3. Watch the gateway log for `[prompt-cache]`.

### Expected behavior

The second consult's request starts with the first consult's last request unchanged, so the cache read stays near the full history.

### Actual behavior

```
[prompt-cache] cache read dropped 123445 -> 10708 runId=talk-realtime-consult-2690… request=1 for
anthropic/claude-opus-5-5 via boundary-aware:anthropic-messages; historyRewrite(message 261 (user)
differs from the previous request; history must be append-only; changed fields: content,
envelope.timestamp, envelope.other, envelope.idempotencyKey, envelope.runtimeContext,
envelope.runtimeContextCarrier); requestGapMs=98077
```

Seen on nearly every consult (request gaps 28–98 s).

**Cause (from the stored transcript and source):**

1. `src/gateway/talk/client-agent-runtime.ts` records the generated consult prompt with `display: false, excludeFromContext: true`. The model receives it during the consult, but `iterateSessionContextEntries` drops it on every later load, so the next consult's history is missing a message the previous request contained.
2. Talk speech rows (`provenance: realtime_voice`) are appended by `appendVoiceTranscript` while the consult runs, so in storage they sit between the consult prompt and its answer, where the consult's own requests never had them.

Stored order for one consult (`transcript_events` sequence numbers):
`824 user (consult prompt, excluded) → 825 runtime-context → 826 user (speech, +0.3 s) → 827 assistant toolCall → 830 toolResult → 832 assistant (speech) → 833 assistant final answer`.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.10-beta.2 (same code on `main` @ fbc99b8c)

### Operating system

Linux (Docker)

### Install method

Docker image `ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.10.10-beta.2`

### Model

anthropic/claude-opus-5-5

### Provider / routing chain

`boundary-aware:anthropic-messages`, 5-minute cache

### Impact and severity

Voice consults were ~57% of this agent's model cost in one day, mostly cache writes caused by this. Measured over 19–21 Oct: 52–82k cache-write tokens per consult, 49–66% cache hit.

With a patch for both causes applied to 2026.10.10-beta.2 (PR to follow): 7 consecutive consults, 93% cache hit, ~3–17k cache-write tokens per consult.

### Additional information

Related: #171227 / #171267 (Anthropic 400 from the same excluded consult prompt), #143017 (other prefix rewrites).

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A managed guest installation can cause pnpm to select the native `.openclaw/.pnpm-store` fallback, after which ordinary workspace synchronization copies disposable package-store files into the canonical project.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Use a managed writable guest project with the maintained common sandbox image, pnpm 12.15.0, no explicit store-directory override, and the normal protected skill mounts. In the observed topology, `/workspace` and `/workspace/.openclaw` are distinct writable bind mounts, with the skill directories mounted read-only.
2. Prepare a tiny standalone package under `.openclaw/tmp/cache-fixture`, with a frozen lockfile and the authentic local distribution archive for `semver@7.8.5`. A local archive allows the normal install to run with guest networking disabled. Retain the complete locked pnpm environment document so package-manager preparation does not require registry access.
3. Launch the normal guest exec tool from `/workspace` and run `cd .openclaw/tmp/cache-fixture && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --prefer-offline`. Do not override HOME or store settings. The shell changes cwd while HOME remains `/workspace`.
4. Observe pnpm's selected store, edit an ordinary project file and an authored sibling under `.openclaw`, then allow normal turn synchronization. Inspect the canonical workspace and read the files in a separate guest turn.

The tool's workdir matters: selecting the nested directory as the exec tool's workdir changes HOME to that directory and exercises a different, excluded scratch-store condition. It does not reproduce the root-launch/shell-`cd` path above.

### Expected behavior

Derived dependency-store contents stay with their producing runtime. Ordinary source files, authored siblings and genuine staged inputs still synchronize, and existing authored-file size limits remain intact. This follows the shared generated-path contract in `docs/gateway/sandboxing/workspace-access.md`.

### Actual behavior

The store and its parent were absent from both the sandbox projection and canonical project before the single install. pnpm successfully selected `/workspace/.openclaw/.pnpm-store/v11`, installed the package and created 54 regular store files totaling 125,641 bytes. After normal synchronization, all 54 files were present in both copies.

A 1,661-byte content-addressed `package.json` object had the same inode as the installed semver file. Its bytes and hash then matched the canonical copy, establishing that the admitted file was genuinely generated package-store content. A separate guest turn retained the authored edits, original staged archive/lock and working semver installation; it also retained the incorrectly synchronized cache object.

### OpenClaw version

Source build `2026.10.9`, exercised Gateway revision `968a3fd87707e17c717024ec9e4f33d548f8c8c8`; workspace source `620e1fb31537ea6a3df583f08173e66607fdd2e5`. The relevant exec HOME/workdir, protected-mount and shared path-classifier code is unchanged between those revisions.

### Operating system

Linux/arm64 Debian trixie-based Docker sandbox on a macOS Gateway host.

### Install method

Source build with an isolated Gateway and managed guest workspace.

### Model

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Provider / routing chain

Normal guest exec, managed sandbox projection and canonical workspace synchronization. Inference-provider identity is not part of the established failure.

### Logs

```text
Packages are hard linked from the content-addressable store to the virtual store.
  Content-addressable store is at: /workspace/.openclaw/.pnpm-store/v11
  Virtual store is at:             node_modules/.pnpm
Progress: resolved 1, reused 0, downloaded 1, added 1, done
```

Here `downloaded 1` is ingestion of the verified local archive; guest networking remained disabled.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The native install completed with exit 0. Store identity, installation metadata, file identity and canonical/projection hashes were checked before and after normal synchronization, followed by a separate read-only guest turn. No cache was manually inserted, copied or inflated, and no mount, HOME, policy or store setting was overridden.

The shared classifier at `src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-path-exclusions.ts` excludes `.local/share/pnpm/store` and `.openclaw/tmp`, but not the fallback root between them. pnpm's native hard-link placement selects that fallback when the normal home store cannot link into the nested project.

### Impact and severity

Disposable dependency bytes become authored-project synchronization payloads. The observed small-package case added 54 unnecessary files; larger dependency stores can encounter the existing result limits. This reproduction did not manufacture a large file or replay a 64 MiB rejection, and it does not establish broader frequency or data loss.

### Additional information

Related: #175956 covered ordinary home-relative package and test-tool roots. This report concerns the distinct native fallback at the exact checkout-root `.openclaw/.pnpm-store`; it does not propose excluding arbitrary directories named `.pnpm-store` or changing pnpm's placement and sandbox protections.

issues.body:
### What happens

A local session-read consistency failure can move an agent turn to the next configured model, even though the failure does not identify a provider problem. A natural guest turn reported `SessionEntryChangedDuringReadError`, then recorded a model fallback with reason `unknown`. That turn eventually completed and preserved its requested output; this report is about unexpected routing, not demonstrated lost work.

### Current reproduction

The behavior is reproduced on `faa38148f2c5ba3fe8f69bd3ae0150c87edf7758` through the production `SessionManager.openModelContextAsync` and `runWithModelFallback` owners. The focused case persists a user input, completes a native session write after each of two context reads, and allows the existing bounded read retry to exhaust. The reader produces `SessionEntryChangedDuringReadError`. With a second model configured, the runner returns a completed result from that second model and records the first attempt as `unknown`. The assertion that the local error should propagate fails.

The read and write implementations, read-admission checks, error classifier and fallback runner are real; model output is a fixed callback. This demonstrates the routing boundary, not the original natural incident's exact invalidating write or provider-request phase. Existing provider-failure and cancellation controls passed separately.

### Expected behavior and scope

A session-read coordination outcome should retain its local identity and must not consume a provider/model fallback. Existing bounded local recovery, current session authority, cancellation, saved input and useful retry guidance should remain intact. Genuine provider failures should continue to use configured fallback.

`src/agents/model-fallback-runner.ts` already states this local-coordination contract. The runtime-coordination names in `src/agents/failover-error.ts` omit `SessionEntryChangedDuringReadError`; the resulting unknown classification reaches the next configured candidate. The original read-conflict producer remains unproven and is separate from this classification defect.

issues.body:
### Summary

On Telegram, a `MEDIA:` line pointing at an existing local PDF inside the gateway media directory is never dispatched. The reply text arrives normally, no document send happens, and nothing is logged: no `outbound send ok ... deliveryKind=document`, no `⚠️ Media failed.` suffix, no error line. The same file delivered immediately through the `message` tool with `attachments` + `asDocument`, so the file, the path and the chat are all valid.

### Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.10.8 (dc2523e), Node v24.22.1
- Linux 6.8.0-147-generic (x64), self-hosted VPS
- Channel: Telegram, account `default`, 1:1 DM (`dmPolicy: allowlist`)
- Media stored under `<state>/media/outbound/`, ~76 KB PDF, well below any size limit

### Steps to reproduce

1. Stage a PDF into `<state>/media/outbound/` (76 KB, A4, 12 pages).
2. Reply in the DM with a normal text body and, as the last line, plain at column 0:

   ```
   MEDIA:/root/<state>/media/outbound/<file>.pdf
   ```

3. Check the journal and the chat.

### Expected

The text plus one document message, and a journal line `[telegram] outbound send ok ... deliveryKind=document`.

### Actual

- The text arrives. No document arrives.
- The journal contains only the agent-side line `[agent:nested] ... Attachment: /root/<state>/media/outbound/<file>.pdf` and `outbound send ok ... deliveryKind=text`. There is no `deliveryKind=document` line at all.
- `grep -c "deliveryKind=document"` over the whole day's journal: **0**, across three separate `MEDIA:` attempts on the same account.
- No `⚠️ Media failed.` suffix is appended to the reply text, so the failure is completely invisible to the user (this differs from #103000, where the media is rejected during normalization and the suffix appears).
- In one attempt the attachment was not even copied into `media/outbound/` by the delivery path, while a later attempt did produce the uuid-suffixed copy — and still no document send.

### Workaround

Calling the message tool directly delivers the same file on the first attempt:

```
message({action:"send", channel:"telegram", target:"<chatId>", message:"<caption>",
         attachments:[{type:"file", media:"<path>", name:"<name>", mimeType:"application/pdf"}],
         asDocument:true})
```

returns `{"ok":true,"messageId":"…","messageDelivery":{"status":"settled"}}` and the document arrives.

### Why this is not a duplicate

- #185547: media load failure drops the **text** reply. Here the text is delivered and only the file is missing.
- #180556: `MEDIA:` line is dropped when text follows **on the same line** under block streaming. Here `MEDIA:` is the last line, standalone, and streaming is not configured.
- #103000: the drop is logged only at verbose level and the reply shows `⚠️ Media failed.`. Here no rejection occurs and no warning is shown, so even the verbose trace may not exist.

### Impact

Any agent that answers with a file and trusts the `MEDIA:` contract silently loses the attachment while the user sees a complete-looking reply. Because nothing is logged, the agent has no way to detect the loss without reading the journal out of band.

issues.body:
### Problem

`evaluateToolLoopCall` early-returns unless `ctx.loopDetection?.enabled === true` (`src/agents/tool-loop-admission.ts:33-35`). The config field is optional and defaults to false (`src/config/zod-schema.agent-runtime.ts:425-430`; the schema help says "Omit to keep rolling detection off"). The run loop is `while (true)` with exits only on model stop, abort or intervention (`packages/agent-core/src/agent-loop.ts:221`) — there is **no `maxTurns` and no token budget**.

Even with detection enabled, the thresholds allow ~10 identical calls before a warning, 20 before critical and 30 before the circuit breaker (`src/agents/tool-loop-detection.ts:55-57`) ≈ 25K/100K/150K tokens at a 5K-token context. With the default (off) the spend is unbounded. The only always-on brake is `observeRepeatedToolError` (3 identical **error** outcomes, `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/tool-loop-recovery.ts:27-46`) — successful-but-useless calls never trip it.

A second, related gap: there is **no proactive token or cost budget** anywhere. `src/agents/usage.ts` (459 lines) is pure normalisation and accounting; the only quota surface derives `quota_exhausted` *after* the provider returns `rate_limit` (`src/agents/session-suspension.ts:59-66`).

**The same gap has a second face: what is already in the context keeps being re-billed.** `applyContextPruningDefaults` only materialises `contextPruning` defaults when `hasAnthropicDefaultSignal(cfg, env)` is true (`src/config/defaults.ts:539-541`; the function starts at `:531`), and `resolveCacheTtlPruningSettings` returns `undefined` for non-`cache-ttl` modes (`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.ts:56-58`) — so on a non-Anthropic install **no old-tool-result reducer runs at all**, and `limitHistoryTurns` no-ops on an undefined limit (`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/history.ts:26-28`). Every retained tool result (per-result cap 16K/32K/64K chars ≈ 4K/8K/16K tokens, `src/agents/tool-result-limits.ts:5-26`) is re-serialised into every request until compaction: 40 × 16K-char results ≈ 640K chars ≈ **160K tokens re-billed per turn** (*estimate*; cached reads still cost).

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# a task that makes the model call the same tool repeatedly with successful outcomes
# -> no brake, no cap, unbounded spend
```

### Expected behavior

A run has a ceiling, and the loop brake is on unless the operator explicitly turns it off.

### Actual behavior

Both brakes are off by default, and a repetitive-but-successful tool loop is bounded by nothing but the provider's own rate limit and the operator's wallet.

### Environment

- OpenClaw `v2026.10.10-beta.2`, commit `2b85c4c25ea98d72ca1d3e93fb0fd9cac8f0ddab`

### Evidence

- `src/agents/tool-loop-admission.ts:33-35`
- `src/config/zod-schema.agent-runtime.ts:425-430`, `src/config/schema.help.runtime.ts:445`
- `packages/agent-core/src/agent-loop.ts:221`
- `src/agents/tool-loop-detection.ts:55-57`
- `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/tool-loop-recovery.ts:27-46`
- `src/agents/usage.ts`, `src/agents/session-suspension.ts:59-66`

### Proposed solution

1. Flip the admission gate to `enabled !== false`, or default `tools.loopDetection.enabled: true` in the config defaults.
2. Add a per-run tool-call budget (e.g. 60 calls) enforced in `packages/agent-core/src/agent-loop.ts` regardless of the detection configuration.
3. Optionally add `agents.defaults.budgets.{dailyTokens,dailyCost}` checked at run admission against the existing usage sink, suspending through the existing `QuotaSuspension` path. No API change.
4. **Bound what is already in the context:** default `contextPruning: { mode: "cache-ttl", ttl: "1h" }` for all providers (or a pressure-mode prune at ≥ 15 % window fill) and a default `historyLimit` (e.g. 40 turns). `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/history.ts:44-47` already evicts in batches specifically to keep the cache prefix stable, so a default limit is cache-safe. On a non-Anthropic install this is the difference between re-billing ~160K tokens of tool results per turn and not.

### Why this is not a PR from the audit

Turning the brake on by default changes behaviour for every operator, and the right ceiling is a product decision (a low ceiling breaks legitimate long tasks; a high one does not protect the budget). The maintainers should set the default.

---

issues.body:
## Summary

Background Skill Workshop reviews cost credits two ways, and neither is covered by #173889:

1. **Every skill the review edits changes the reusable prompt prefix** of the running session.
2. **The review session itself never reuses its own cache**, because its history is rewritten each pass.

Together these dropped ~16.7M tokens in a single evening on one deployment.

## Environment

- Prefix-caching deployment, self-hosted Gateway, gateway with a turn subscription plan
- Workshop `skills.workshop.autonomous.mode: "auto"` (default)
- Observed 2026-10-19, 20:36-23:03 CST
- OpenClaw **2026.10.5** (build `1b58cb9`)
- Prefix-caching routes observed on this deployment: `anthropic-messages` and `openai-completions`

## Vector 1 - learned-skill metadata sits at the head of the system prompt

Learned skills are surfaced into the system prompt as `name` + `description` + path. That is the *earliest* cacheable segment of the prompt, so editing one description string invalidates the entire reusable prefix for the next turn - even though the conversation body is unchanged.

Between 20:36 and 23:03, **9 skill files were edited**. The main session recorded **37 cache drops, 27 of them larger than 100k tokens** (typical 230k-400k per drop).

This is a different insertion point from the runtime-context-at-tail behavior in #158898, but the same class: mutable content placed inside the reusable prefix.

## Vector 2 - the review session's own cache never survives

The background review forks the conversation and its history is rewritten on each pass, so its own prefix is discarded every time:

```
20:36:36   466432 -> 0
20:47:19   510208 -> 1024
22:36:43   576256 -> 15360
22:59:39   585984 -> 16384
```

Totals for the window:

| session | tokens dropped |
|---|---|
| review session | 7.71M |
| main session | 9.0M |
| **combined** | **~16.7M** |

## Timestamps align

```
20:36:10  windows-wrapper-script        -> main   20:40:42  269312 -> 1024
                                          review 20:36:36  466432 -> 0      (+6s)
20:46:45  openclaw-plugin-update       -> main   20:46:44  279552 -> 1024
20:47:58  openclaw-update-install-fail -> review 20:47:19  510208 -> 1024
22:51:41  lossless-claw-maintenance    -> review 22:59:39  585984 -> 16384
```

## The review reviews the *entire* conversation

This is the structural reason the cost scales badly, and it is the part that seems hardest to justify.

A background Skill Workshop review is not scoped to the turn that triggered it. It forks the conversation and reviews the whole of it. An assistant session is normally long-running, so the cost of "review my recent work" grows with **session length** instead of staying bounded.

Concretely on this deployment: after context compaction had already brought the main session down to **~300k tokens**, a background review was observed running with a context of **~500k tokens** - larger than the session that triggered it - and this recurred across multiple reviews in the same window.

That also appears to be in tension with #173889, which states a cap of at most 64 events / 32 KiB. The most likely reading is that the cap bounds what the review **reads**, not the size of the **request** that carries the forked conversation. If so, the transport cost of every review still scales with session length even though the reviewed slice is small.

A housekeeping task that runs in the background on every qualifying turn should not be able to exceed the context of the session that scheduled it.

## What #173889 already fixed, and what it does not

#173889 correctly bounded the *per-review* cost: at most 64 events / 32 KiB, `skill_workshop` as the only exposed tool, bootstrap/catalog/client instructions and cache/delivery context stripped, low reasoning, 2048 output tokens, and 15/30/60-minute backoff after rate limiting.

That bounds one review. It does not address:

- **Frequency.** The counter is 10 model iterations per session, but a single user message that uses 12-24 tool calls already produces 12-24 iterations. On this host, 48 user messages produced **235 model iterations**. In addition, any turn that *read* a learned skill queues a review regardless of the counter.
- **Prefix invalidation** caused by the resulting skill edits (Vector 1).
- **The review session's own cache** (Vector 2).

## Requested behavior

1. **Return background review to a schedule** rather than firing every 10 model iterations.
2. **Or gate reviews on actual skill usage** - e.g. review a skill only after it has been used N times, or after a correction was observed on it - instead of on raw iteration count.
3. **Consider placing the learned-skill catalog outside the reusable prefix** (or emitting descriptions only when they change), so a skill edit does not invalidate the whole conversation prefix.
4. **Avoid rewriting the review session's history** between passes, so its own cache can be reused.
5. **Scope a review to the turns that actually changed** instead of the whole session, so review cost does not scale with session length. A truncated or incremental review is acceptable - reviewing the turns since the previous review would cover the same lessons.

Config note: `skills.workshop.autonomous.mode: "off"` stops the reviews, and `/learn`, prompted skill creation, and *Learn from history* remain available - so the mechanism can be deferred without losing the ability to save lessons.

## Related

- #158898 - runtime context message appended last on every model call (same class, different insertion point)
- #172313 - fix(agents): source metadata changes invalidate the reusable prompt prefix
- #141969 - mid-turn overflow recovery and silent exec completion cause full-context LLM reruns
- #173889 - fix(skills): keep background reviews out of saturated token budgets
- #176227 - tools.toolsBySender changes the tool list and system prompt, so the prompt cache misses

issues.body:
### Summary

Automation (cron) job state changes are not recorded in any audit trail: create, edit, enable, disable, remove. Someone or something can turn a job back on, and afterwards nobody can tell who, from where, or when.

### Version

OpenClaw 2026.9.4 (3a9d69d), macOS arm64, single gateway, multi-agent.

### What happened

We paused 14 automation jobs on purpose with `openclaw automations disable <id>`. Over the next several hours, every one of them was switched back to `enabled: true`, one job at a time, at different times. We could not find out what did it.

- `config-audit` and `system-agent-audit` in `diagnostic_events` (documented in cli/openclaw.md, "Change history") are recording normally. But automation jobs live in the shared SQLite state database, not `openclaw.json`, so the config journal never sees these changes.
- `openclaw audit` (kinds `agent_run`, `tool_action`, `message`) did not show an enable call against these jobs that we could attribute.
- `openclaw automations runs <id>` shows when each job *executed*, not when its configuration changed.

The only evidence we have is indirect: gaps in run history show roughly when each job resumed.

### Expected

Every change to an automation job's state goes to an append-only audit scope (for example, `automation-audit` in `diagnostic_events`, alongside `config-audit`). Each record includes:

- the job id and the operation (`add`, `edit`, `enable`, `disable`, `remove`, plus auto-disable and auto-delete events from the scheduler itself)
- the changed fields (paths, as config-audit does), before and after for `enabled`
- the actor/origin: CLI (and user), Control UI, agent tool call (agent id, session key, run id), scheduler-internal, or doctor/migration
- a timestamp

A way to read it back: `openclaw audit --kind automation_change`, or `openclaw automations history <id>`.

### Why it matters

The pause was a deliberate safety lockdown on jobs that write to long-term memory. Because a disabled job can be silently re-enabled, disabling is not a reliable control. We worked around this by polling `automations list --all --json` every 5 minutes and diffing the `enabled` flags. A built-in audit record would make that unnecessary, and would have named the cause directly.

### Nice to have

Optionally, protect a job against being re-enabled unless the caller passes an explicit override flag. For example, `automations disable <id> --lock "<reason>"`, so that a later enable requires `--unlock` and is recorded in the audit.

issues.body:
# `skill_workshop` background experience-review retries repeatedly on invalid tool-call arguments, no visible retry/turn cap

## Summary

OpenClaw's automatic post-conversation "experience review" (spawned as `agent:main:internal-session-effects:skill-workshop-review_<uuid>` sessions, using the `skill_workshop` tool) repeatedly produced invalid tool-call arguments for `skill_workshop` and had to retry, burning real paid model calls each time. Observed on `2026.10.5` against a real IONOS AI Model Hub-backed model (`Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B`) immediately after upgrading from an earlier `2026.10.x` build.

## What we saw

Over one afternoon, 8 separate `skill-workshop-review` sessions ran (one per preceding real conversation turn), together issuing 60 real `skill_workshop` tool calls and consuming ~11.7M real tokens. Of those, at least 4 sessions hit a schema-validation failure:

```
tool_call failed: Invalid arguments for tool "openclaw:core:skill_workshop": <root>: must not have additional properties: "description", "evidence". Expected input: { action: "list" | "view" | "create" | "patch" | "write_file" | "remove_file" | "archive" | "restore"; absorbed_into?: string; content?: string; file_path?: string; name?: string; new_text?: string; old_text?: string; reason?: string; version?: string }.
```

```
tool_call failed: Invalid arguments for tool "openclaw:core:skill_workshop": <root>: must not have additional properties: "evidence", "skill_name"; action: must be equal to one of the allowed values (allowed: "list", "view", "create", "patch", "write_file", "remove_file", "archive", "restore").
```
(raw args used `"action":"update"` — not a member of the allowed enum — together with `evidence`, `skill_name`, `expected_revision`, `proposal_content`, `description` fields that don't exist on the schema at all)

```
tool_call failed: Invalid arguments for tool "openclaw:core:skill_workshop": <root>: must not have additional properties: "expected_revision", "proposal_content", "skill_name"; action: must be equal to one of the allowed values (...).
```

```
tool_call failed: Invalid arguments for tool "openclaw:core:skill_workshop": <root>: must not have additional properties: "proposal_content".
```

Each failure consumed a full real model call before the next retry (confirmed from per-call token telemetry — these aren't free/local validation-only retries). One session needed 11 separate `skill_workshop` tool calls before completing.

We checked the system prompt that drives these review sessions (`experience-review-*.mjs` in the installed package) — it correctly only mentions `action=list`/`view`/`patch` and a `reason` field, and never mentions `update`, `evidence`, `description`, `proposal_content`, `expected_revision`, or `skill_name`. So this doesn't look like a prompt/schema version mismatch on OpenClaw's side — the model itself (in this case `Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B`, a non-first-party model routed through IONOS AI Model Hub) is repeatedly inventing a richer "proposal/evidence" change-workflow that doesn't exist in the real tool schema, across multiple independent review sessions. In our own experience this particular model is prone to inventing plausible-but-nonexistent parameters/options in general (not specific to this tool), so we don't think this points at a prompt/schema bug — it's raised purely as operational feedback on a fully internal, user-invisible background feature, not a request to change behavior for this model specifically.

## Why we're flagging it anyway

Regardless of whether the root cause is model-side tool-call weakness or something about how the schema/examples are presented, this is a background, automatically-scheduled feature (not something the user directly asked for) that is:
- burning real, billed tokens on invalid retries with no cap we could find in the installed build on these failed arguments, and
- not surfaced anywhere the user would notice (it runs silently as an internal-session-effect; we only found it via telemetry while investigating unrelated metrics accuracy).

Two independent, lower-risk mitigations that seem worth considering regardless of root cause:
1. A max-retry / max-turn budget specifically for `skill_workshop` background review sessions, so a model stuck re-guessing invalid arguments gives up after N attempts instead of continuing to spend real tokens.
2. Including the exact allowed `action` enum and property list directly in the `skill_workshop` tool's description/schema docstring (not just the validator's rejection message), which may reduce how often a model has to discover the real schema via trial-and-error error messages.

## Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.10.5` (`1b58cb9`), upgraded same-day from an earlier `2026.10.x` build
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B` via IONOS AI Model Hub (OpenAI-compatible endpoint)
- Plugin: `th-m-vogel/openclaw-observability-plugin` (OTel observability plugin, fork) — used only to gather this telemetry, not implicated in the behavior itself
