prs.title: fix: scheduled automations keep running after their Telegram account is removed while a binding remains
prs.body:
Related #187513 (partial repair; the issue stays open for the cases below).

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: capped automations created from a named Telegram account keep running under the channel's base group policy after that account is removed, when a binding still names it. `openclaw channels remove --delete` leaves that binding behind, and when the removed account was the last named one while the channel keeps its own bot token, the leftover binding turns the removed id into a served single-bot alias.

## User Impact

User impact: after a named (non-default) Telegram account is removed, its capped automations stop with `Scheduled account "<id>" is unavailable`, as the cron troubleshooting docs already describe, instead of running with tools the operator had denied on that account. When `channels remove --delete` or `openclaw configure` removes the last entry from `channels.telegram.accounts`, the bindings that name non-default accounts are removed as well, in a second write after the account delete. Every delete that succeeds on main still succeeds with the same exit status: the account delete is the same write main makes, and when the bindings cannot be updated the command prints a warning naming what to check and the delete is kept. Configured accounts, the single-bot layout (channel bot token plus a binding, no `accounts` map), deletes that leave an account entry in place, and other channels behave as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

The scheduled creator-account check from #115932 asks the channel whether the account is listed. Telegram also lists ids that bindings name, so a removed account can stay listed. Three changes:

- Channel config adapters get an optional synchronous `hasAccountConfig(cfg, accountId)`. The check now requires a listed id and, when the adapter provides the hook, a `true` result (a throw or any other value refuses). Telegram wires its existing `hasTelegramAccountConfig`, the predicate its conversation route ownership already uses: a binding-only id is not an account while other named accounts exist. Adapters without the hook keep today's behavior; the read-only channel alias wrapper rebinds the hook like the other config readers.
- Once `channels.telegram.accounts` is empty, a channel bot token (present, or added later with `channels add`) serves every bound id, so the predicate cannot tell a removed id from an intended alias. Telegram's `deleteAccount` therefore drops the bindings (route or ACP) that name non-default accounts when a delete removes the last entry from that map. Deletes that leave an account entry in place do not touch bindings.
- The config writer lets one `$include` file own each write and refuses a write that shrinks the file below half its size unless the caller allows it. A single write that both deletes the account and drops bindings therefore failed where main's account-only delete succeeds: when `channels.telegram` and `bindings` come from different files, and on small configs. `channels remove --delete` and `openclaw configure` now save the delete's changes under `channels` exactly as before, then write its other changes (the bindings) to the same config file in a second write. That second write runs only while the account is still deleted and the bindings are still what the delete saw; it allows the size drop for itself only; and a list that its own `$include` file holds is emptied in that file instead of being removed from the root file.

Left out: a Doctor finding for bindings that name a missing account, and removals that bypass `deleteAccount` (`openclaw configure` → Remove channel config, `config unset`, hand edits): removing the last account entry that way leaves its bindings, which a channel bot token then serves.

Remaining case for owners: when the second write is refused or skipped, the delete is kept and the command warns. While a binding still names a removed id, the account map is empty and the channel has its own bot token (kept from before the delete, or set later, for example by `channels add` for the default account), that token serves the id again, so its capped automations keep running under the channel's settings, as they do on main after every such delete. The bindings stay only when the writer cannot update them (for example an array-entry, multi-file or external `$include`, or a root `$include` with sibling keys) or when values were edited between the writes. The warning asks to check the bindings, `docs/cli/channels.md` states these conditions, and removing the binding restores the refusal. Two fail-closed variants were tried and not kept: refusing the delete turns a delete main completes into a failure, and keeping an explicit `accounts: { default: {} }` entry makes later setup treat the channel as multi-account (a later `channels add` leaves the webhook and DM / group policy at the channel level, where the new bot inherits them).

## Evidence

Built Gateway, real Telegram plugin against a loopback Bot API stub, token auth, capped automation created from a Telegram group by an owner, `cron.run` force per phase; main vs this branch:

| Phase | main | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| A configured account | ok, `read` offered | ok, `read` offered |
| N account denies `read` | ok, `read` not offered | ok, `read` not offered |
| R account removed (another account remains), binding kept | ok, `read` offered again | error `Scheduled account "team" is unavailable`, 0 model requests |
| R last named account removed with `channels remove --delete`, channel bot token kept | ok, `read` offered again | error `Scheduled account "team" is unavailable`, 0 model requests; only `default` running afterwards |
| R account removed, no binding | error, 0 model requests | error, 0 model requests |

The last-account row was re-run on this branch before the last refactor of `openclaw configure`'s call site, which does not touch the `channels remove` path; the other rows exercise the scheduled check, which this revision does not change.

Built CLI `channels remove --channel telegram --account <id> --delete` on each layout (built before that refactor), then the scheduled check (production `resolveGroupToolPolicy`, real Telegram plugin) for every removed id on the written config.

| Layout, deletes | main: exit / bindings left / check | this branch: exit / bindings left / check |
|---|---|---|
| another named account remains, remove `team` | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0 / `team` / refused |
| last named account, channel bot token | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0 / none / refused |
| last named account, no channel token | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0 / none / refused |
| `channels.telegram` from an `$include` file, last account | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0 / none / refused |
| `bindings` from an `$include` file, last account | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0 / emptied in its file / refused |
| both from separate `$include` files, last account | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0 / emptied in its file / refused |
| `channels.telegram` from an `$include` file, another account remains | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0 / `team` / refused |
| remove `alpha`, then `beta` (about 600 bytes) | 0, 0 / `alpha`, `beta` / admitted | 0, 0 / none / refused |
| remove `ops`, then `default` (about 600 bytes) | 0, 0 / `ops` / admitted | 0, 0 / none / refused |
| last account with six named bindings (about 1 KB) | 0 / all six / admitted | 0 / none / refused (all six ids) |

Built CLI `openclaw configure --section channels` driven through a terminal (Delete config), main vs this branch (built at 49d7ccce996; the last commit changes only text), then the same scheduled check on each written config. In both tables, settings outside `channels.telegram` and `bindings` came out unchanged on both sides.

| Layout, deleted with `openclaw configure` | main: exit / bindings left / check | this branch: exit / bindings left / check |
|---|---|---|
| last named account, channel bot token | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0 / none / refused |
| last named account, no channel token | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0 / none / refused |
| another named account remains | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0 / `team` / refused |
| `bindings` from an `$include` file, last account | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0 / emptied in its file / refused |
| last account with six named bindings (about 650 bytes) | 0 / all six / admitted | 0 / none / refused |
| remove `alpha`, then `beta` in one session (1.1 KB) | 0 / `alpha`, `beta` / admitted | 0 / none / refused |
| binding from an array-entry `$include`, last account | 0 / `team` / admitted | 0, warning / `team` / admitted |
| `channels.telegram` or the whole config from an `$include` file (4 layouts) | 1, nothing written | 1, same writer message, nothing written |

Upgrade from the latest release, 2026.10.9, on one state: the release's CLI wrote every Telegram, binding and owner setting (accounts `default`, `team`, `keep`, a `team` binding, `team`'s group policy, the owner; the harness set the rest), and its Gateway created a capped automation from a group message (mode `account`, owner `team`) whose forced run offered `read`. This head's `doctor --fix --non-interactive` exited 0 (changing only `agents`, `meta` and `wizard`) and `config validate` passed; its Gateway listed the same automation with its definition, owner and policy unchanged, and the forced run offered `read`; after `channels remove --delete` of `team` (`default` and `keep` remain, so the binding stays), the next run failed with `Scheduled account "team" is unavailable`, 0 model requests.

The 2026.10.9 CLI also wrote three configs: accounts `default`, `team`, `keep` with bindings; a channel bot token with an `alias` binding and no `accounts` map; a channel bot token plus account `team` (set with `config set`) and its binding. Main and this head ran `doctor --fix`, `config validate` (passed) and the same commands: every config came out identical apart from a doctor timestamp and this head's intended drop of `team`'s binding (last named account deleted beside the channel token). The scheduled check admits every configured id and `alias` on both; after the deletes main still admits every removed id, this head refuses them.

PR test files on main (554f0b886bd, the PR base) vs this head:

| File (cases) | main | this head |
|---|---|---|
| `agent-tools.policy.account-config` (5) | 4 fail on `expected [Function] to throw an error`; the no-predicate case passes | 5/5 pass |
| `telegram/src/config-adapter` (12) | 4 delete cases fail on kept bindings (e.g. `expected [ Array(1) ] to be undefined`); 2 stop at the missing hook (`undefined`); 6 unchanged cases pass | 12/12 pass |
| `read-only.writers` (new case) | `expected false to be true` (hook not rebound for the alias) | 3/3 pass |
| `channels.remove` (new case) | `expected [ 'channel write' ] to deeply equal [ 'channel write', 'follow-up' ]` | 14/14 pass |

prs.title: fix(cli): message read loads every plugin when the channel plugin is external
prs.body:
Closes #185280

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw message read --channel discord` loads the full plugin registry locally (about 0.5 GB and 20+ s of CPU per call) when Discord is installed as an external npm plugin. The Gateway already owns the action.

## User Impact

User impact: Gateway-owned `message` actions on external channel plugins now go straight to the Gateway without loading the plugin locally. A `message read` against npm-installed Discord drops from about 27 s wall / 31 s CPU / 526 MB to about 11 s wall / 12 s CPU / 430 MB on our host. The remaining time is CLI startup; plugin loading is gone (see Evidence).

**Risk: this adds a public manifest field**, `channelConfigs.<id>.gatewayMessageActions` (documented in `docs/plugins/manifest/surfaces.md`).
- It is optional. It is used only when the channel plugin is neither bundled nor loaded in the CLI process. A bundled or loaded plugin's `actions.resolveExecutionMode` still decides.
- An external plugin's manifest is untrusted data. Here it only chooses the Gateway route. The Gateway still runs its own account, target, and read-authority checks with its loaded plugin.
- Existing external Discord installs benefit after the next `@openclaw/discord` release that ships this manifest. Older plugin packages keep today's behavior.
- An undeclared action to an external channel now runs one extra validate-only config pass and one metadata snapshot read (~0.2 s) before the existing local preload.

## Why This Change Was Made

Fixing `isGatewayOwnedMessageAction` alone does not help. With the predicate forced to `true` on `main`, `runMessageAction` → `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin({ allowBootstrap: true })` still bootstraps the plugin, measured at 14.4 s / 596 MB. The message route needs a channel plugin object, even for actions it only forwards to `message.action`.

So the decision moves into manifest metadata, and the route gets a plugin object that needs no runtime:

- The manifest mirrors the actions the runtime adapter sends to the Gateway. A Discord test keeps the list equal to the discovered actions whose `resolveExecutionMode` is `"gateway"`, so the runtime adapter stays the single owner.
- When the scoped channel plugin is not available locally, the message CLI asks the existing runtime-free manifest channel adapter (`src/channels/plugins/read-only.ts`). For a declared action, it returns that adapter with Gateway-only `actions` and `outbound.deliveryMode: "gateway"`. The CLI passes it to the normal `runMessageAction` through the scoped plugin registry, so routing, target, account, and policy code is shared, not duplicated.
- Dry-runs, broadcasts, and undeclared actions keep the current local preparation path.

Production +190/−21 (including the 38-line Discord manifest entry and one line in `scripts/pr-lib/wrapper-components.txt`, because the manifest normalizer now imports `src/channels/plugins/message-action-names.ts`), tests +100, docs +15/−9.

The delegated adapter reads the normalized, typed `record.channelConfigs` with an own-property check, so it adds no type assertions.

## Evidence

**Before/after measurement** (taken on the first revision; the review repairs do not touch the runtime path). Release-shaped packages built with `scripts/package-openclaw-for-docker.mjs` from `main` (`ed141d0198`) and from this branch, so Discord is not bundled. Both runs use:
- the same `@openclaw/discord` package, built from this branch with `scripts/plugin-npm-publish.sh --pack` (the old core ignores the new field)
- a separate isolated `OPENCLAW_HOME` per variant
- a loopback test Gateway on port 28789

Command: `openclaw message read --channel discord --target channel:123456789012345678 --limit 1 --json`, 3 runs each, measured with `/usr/bin/time`.

Every run reaches the test Gateway's `message.action`, which the Discord plugin rejects with "read target channel is not allowed" (dummy token, allowlist policy). So all six runs exercise the same CLI → Gateway path. The host was busy (load average ~8), so absolute times are inflated for both variants.

| Run | Before wall | Before CPU (user+sys) | Before max RSS | After wall | After CPU (user+sys) | After max RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 31.0 s | 35.0 s | 525 MB | 13.4 s | 10.3 s | 431 MB |
| 2 | 25.5 s | 29.7 s | 524 MB | 10.5 s | 13.4 s | 429 MB |
| 3 | 24.3 s | 29.0 s | 528 MB | 9.0 s | 10.8 s | 429 MB |
| **Mean** | **27.0 s** | **31.2 s** | **526 MB** | **11.0 s** | **11.5 s** | **430 MB** |

CPU profiles of one run each:
- Before: `loadPluginRegistryHandle` 24.6 s inclusive, of which `createPluginGenerationArtifact` is 17.4 s.
- After: `loadPluginRegistryHandle` and `bootstrapOutboundChannelPlugin` 0 ms, `resolveGatewayDelegatedChannelPlugin` 0.2 s, `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshot` 1.2 s. The rest is CLI module loading.

**Tests.** Each of these was red before the fix.
- `src/cli/program/message/helpers.test.ts`: a read on an external channel whose manifest delegates it skips `loadPluginRegistryHandle`, runs config-ready in validate-only mode, and runs `messageCommand` against the delegated adapter. Undeclared actions still finish full config-ready and preload. 53 passed.
- `src/channels/plugins/read-only.test.ts`: a delegated read through the real `runMessageAction` reaches `message.action` with no runtime or setup load (fixture markers). This caught the outbound bootstrap during development. The same test checks that undeclared actions and disabled plugins are not delegated. 30 passed (the three delegation cases are folded into one regression; it goes red when `outbound.deliveryMode: "gateway"` is removed).
- `extensions/discord/src/channel-actions.test.ts`: the manifest list equals Discord's discovered Gateway-mode actions. 12 passed.
- Also run after the rebase: `src/plugins/manifest-registry.test.ts` (65), `src/cli/program/register.message.test.ts` (10), `src/cli/program/message/register.read-edit-delete.test.ts` (5 + 1 skipped), `src/cli/program/message/register.thread.test.ts` (6), all passed.

**Review repairs** (now rebased onto `a4e20a8b244`):
- The wrapper inventory now lists `src/channels/plugins/message-action-names.ts`. `test/scripts/pr-worktree-provision.test.ts` (16 + 2 skipped), `test/scripts/eager-import-closure.test.ts` (35) and `test/scripts/pr-wrapper-source-closure.test.ts` (3) pass; they failed in CI on `e81e39d81d`.
- The Gateway request mock in `read-only.test.ts` is an untyped `vi.fn()`. A `vi.fn<NonNullable<OutboundMessageGatewayOptionsInput["request"]>>()` still fails `tsgo` (TS2322): Vitest's `Mock<T>` takes `ReturnType<T>`, which turns the generic `Promise<T>` into `Promise<unknown>`. Untyped `vi.fn()` has no cast and is the pattern in `src/infra/approval-gateway-resolver.test.ts`.
- `pnpm check:assertion-safety` and `pnpm check:max-lines-ratchet` pass against `3c64f85073`.
- `src/plugins/bundled-plugin-categories.test.ts` failed on `e81e39d81d` because the old merge base `ed141d0198` shipped `extensions/knowledge/openclaw.plugin.json` without `categories`; `main` fixed that in 0957af2568, and the test passes after the rebase.
- Test-line growth is +100 (down from +135) after folding the new cases into existing suites without dropping any assertion. `check-test-lines-ratchet.mts --base <main> --no-merge-base` passes against `a4e20a8b244` (6,246,128 of 6,320,000).

**Checks.** `tsgo` passes for `tsconfig.core.json`, `tsconfig.extensions.json`, `test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.plugin-sdk.json` and `test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json`. `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check` pass on the changed files. `scripts/run-oxlint-shards.mts --files-json <changed files>` passes for the core and extensions shards.

**Target names and mentions (`d051165`).** Review found that the runtime-free delegated adapter has no target grammar: a mention such as `<@123456789012345678>` was rejected in the CLI (`Unknown target …`), and a channel name such as `#name` reached Discord's Gateway `read` handler unresolved and was refused (`Discord read target channel is not allowed.`, seen live on `aa10b3b`; 2026.10.9 reads the same name). Now:
- CLI: when the delegated adapter has neither `messaging` nor `directory`, an operator call (`conversationReadOrigin: "direct-operator"`) defers target lookup to the Gateway (`message-action-routing.ts`).
- Gateway: `message.action` resolves a direct-operator target with its loaded plugin through the existing `resolveMessageTarget` before dispatch, when the plugin has a target resolver or directory. A target that is already canonical resolves to itself, and agent-runtime callers (which resolve before sending) are not rewritten. The send-default target lookup that already lived in `send.ts` moves with it into `message-action-target.ts`, so `send.ts` shrinks (line-cap ratchet).
- Tests, red before and green after: `read-only.test.ts` (a mention now reaches `message.action` unresolved instead of failing in the CLI) and `message-action-target.test.ts` (an operator's `#general` resolves to the plugin's `channel:C42`; a delegated caller's target is left as sent). `send.test.ts` (79), `read-only.test.ts` (30), `send.scheduled-reads.integration.test.ts`, `message-action-runner.plugin-dispatch.test.ts` and `cli/program/message/helpers.test.ts` pass; `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:core:test`, oxlint, oxfmt and `pnpm check:import-cycles` are clean.
- The branch now includes current `main` (merged at `b829a7f`, no conflicts), so it is on a 2026.10.9 base.

**Real bot and upgrade from 2026.10.9 (2026-10-30, head `d051165`).** Release-shaped package of this head (`scripts/package-openclaw-for-docker.mjs`, Discord not bundled) and `@openclaw/discord` packed from this head. Isolated prefix and `OPENCLAW_HOME`, loopback Gateway, a real Discord bot as `channels.discord.accounts.main`, an allowlisted private test channel.
1. Install `openclaw@2026.10.9` and `npm:@openclaw/discord@2026.10.9`; both `--target channel:<id>` and `--target '#<channel name>'` read the latest message.
2. Stop the Gateway and run `openclaw update --tag <this head's tgz> --no-restart --yes` from that install:
   ```
   Update mode: npm / Update target: 2026.10.9
   Admission checks: config: ok, database-schema: ok, node-runtime: ok, plugin-availability: ok.
   Plugins updated; Gateway restart skipped (--no-restart).
   openclaw --version: OpenClaw 2026.10.9 (d051165)
   ```
   `channels` is unchanged (same `accounts.main`, guild and channel allowlist); the only config changes are Doctor's `agents.entries.main` and the `wizard` record. The published Discord plugin stays installed.
   (The first attempt failed in the candidate Doctor because the test's home directory was group-writable: `… writable without sticky protection; … chmod go-w …`. That is current `main`'s state-directory check on my test directory, not this change; after `chmod go-w` on the test directories the same update passes.)
3. With the published 2026.10.9 Discord plugin (no `gatewayMessageActions`), reads take the existing full-load path and both targets work: `channel:<id>` wall 35.5 s / max RSS 486 MB, `#name` 31.4 s / 589 MB.
4. With the Discord plugin packed from this head (`openclaw plugins install <tgz>`), reads take the delegated path and both targets work, two runs each: `channel:<id>` 5.8 s and 5.5 s / 372 MB, `#name` 5.7 s and 4.9 s / 371 MB. Each returns the same latest message as step 1.

The timings come from a busy host; read them only as a check of the measured table above.

_Opened by an AI assistant on the operator's request; measurements are from our own host._

prs.title: fix: preserve saved selections during native status inspection
prs.body:
Related: #177451, #177443.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes native `/status` silently clearing saved account or model selections while inspecting a session. This forward-ports the remaining applicable repair from #177451 to `main`.

## User Impact

Status cards preserve saved selections, including unavailable automatic auth profiles and model pins that are no longer allowed. No configuration change, migration, or user action is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Model selection can normalize saved pins. Status now gives it a private, identity-consistent entry/store snapshot with no persistence path, while rendering the original saved entry. Credit to @montrellcruse for the original fix and regression coverage in #177451.

The release PR's steering changes are not copied: #175837 replaced separate command/conversation reservations with a single retargeted controller input. Current main retains source cancellation and exact native-outcome custody, including negative acknowledgments. Restoring the old reader and queue plumbing would duplicate retired ownership.

Simplification: production +9/-3, one existing owner, no new runtime API or state. The adapted SQLite-backed regression suite uses the real model-selection owner and status renderer; 161 new test lines receive a scoped test-budget allocation. External credential overlays, discovery, and usage I/O are fixture-controlled.

## Evidence

- On base `89db1d0eec9b3`, the new suite reproduces two unwanted persisted mutations: an unavailable automatic auth pin is removed, and a disallowed saved model pin is cleared. Three other auth-pin controls pass. The older release's saved-selection exception does not reproduce on this main.
- With the fix, all 16 focused checks passed: read-only status (5), status authorization/reasoning (5), and Discord direct-status delivery (6). Combined wall time: 36.47 seconds; read-only test bodies: 5.34 seconds; final fixture recheck: 5/5 in 39.19 seconds including worker preparation. CI seconds are not yet available.
- Focused plugin-SDK TypeScript check, scoped lint/format, whitespace check, and test-line budget and mock-export ratchets pass.
- Independent source review: no material findings. Local ClawSweeper committed-range review of `89db1d0eec9b3..05a15557063acd023a12a655e4fddba222192cb2`: complete, no material correctness or security findings, high confidence. Tests were not independently rerun by the reviewer.
- This is isolated production-owner/SQLite/renderer proof, not a new live Discord acceptance run. Original release-branch live proof remains scoped to #177451's named builds; no live Gateway was modified.

prs.title: fix(cron): stream batch is lost when its fire meets a locked state database
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A stream schedule (`schedule.kind: "stream"`) drops a batch for good when its fire rejects because the state database stayed locked past its 5 s busy timeout. `classifyFireOutcome` records any rejected fire as `payload-error` and discards the batch. Only the `busy` disposition is re-queued.

Observed on a 2026.10.6 Gateway. The run had not started, but the batch was gone (`streamDroppedBatches` 0 → 1) and was never retried:

```
sqlite/transaction  SQLite transaction lock wait failed  {"operation":"cron.schedule-unowned","step":"begin","elapsedMs":5011,"failureKind":"lock-contention","sqliteErrcode":5,"beginAdmission":{"nativeAttempts":1,"nativeMs":5007,"serviceCalls":0}}
cron                cron-stream: batch fire failed       {"err":"Error: database is locked"}
```

The lock holder was the Gateway's own worker thread. It held the WAL write lock while sitting in `fsync` (thread state `D`, wchan `jbd2_log_wait_commit`) during a host-wide disk stall. 4 KB `fsync` calls on that filesystem took 5–34 s at the time. Several Gateways on the same host, each with its own state DB, failed in the same seconds, so this is lock contention caused by slow I/O, not a stray second writer.

## User Impact

When a fire hits a locked state database, the stream batch is now kept as the pending batch. Each retry waits at least 5 s, 10 s and then 20 s after the rejection, and never sooner than the stream's normal cadence (30 s minimum interval in production), so retries start roughly 30, 60 and 90 s apart under sustained contention. A busy settlement between lock rejections keeps the retries the batch has already spent. If the database is still locked on the fourth attempt, the batch is counted as lost exactly as before.

Other rejected fires, and the `error` and `dropped` dispositions, behave as before. No configuration, schema or public API changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

- A lock error here comes from a step that never started the run, such as reserving or scheduling it. The batch is therefore unconsumed and safe to deliver again.
- Errors raised while the job executes do not reach this code. `run-queue-execution.ts` catches them into the run result, so they become a disposition, not a rejection.
- The retry reuses the existing pending-batch path that `busy` already uses, with a bounded backoff applied through `nextEligibleAttemptAtMs`.
- `classifyGatewayStorageFailure` decides what counts as a lock error. It walks wrapped causes and the worker error envelope, and it already maps "outcome unknown" worker failures to `session_actor_reconciliation`. Those are therefore not retried.

- Review found one such path: `requestManualCronRun` commits the run request (`cron.requestRuns`) and then awaits `drainCronRunQueue`. If that drain hit a locked database, the error reached the caller although the request was already durable and a later drain runs it, so the stream retry would have submitted the same batch again. `d7aa4c6` fixes this at the cron owner: once a request is committed, a failed drain is logged (`cron: queue drain delayed`) and the caller waits on the request's completion instead of getting the error. Event-backed requests are unchanged; the drain already settles them through their completion. With that, a lock rejection that reaches the stream comes from a step before the request was accepted.
- The second such path: `launchCronRun` reports the trigger disposition before it awaits `cron.finalizeRuns`. If that completion write fails (for example `SQLITE_BUSY`), the run's completion rejects after the payload already ran, and the stream would have queued the consumed batch again. `4bda208` fixes this in `fireStreamJob`: once a disposition is reported, a later rejection returns that disposition, and the failed completion write stays with cron's receipt recovery.

**Accepted edge case:** the retry count stays bounded in case another post-acceptance path exists. A run whose completion write failed stays marked running until cron's receipt recovery settles it, so later batches report `busy` meanwhile; that is cron's existing lost-result behavior and is unchanged here.

## Evidence

- `src/gateway/cron-stream-output.test.ts` has two new tests:
  - A fire rejected once with `ERR_SQLITE_ERROR` / `errcode: 5` is fired again with the same batch once the 5 s floor has passed (the test uses a 1 ms cadence), and no drop is recorded.
  - Lock and busy outcomes alternating on the same batch do not refill its retry budget: after the fourth lock rejection the batch is counted as lost.
  - A database that stays locked through every retry gives 4 fires and then `streamDroppedBatches: 1`.
  - Both tests fail on `main` (805891d5d3) and pass with this change.
- `src/cron/service.run-queue.test.ts` › "keeps a committed manual run for the next drain when its drain meets a locked database": the first `cron.drainQueue` after a forced run's commit rejects with `database is locked`. Before `d7aa4c6` the run promise rejects with that error; with it, the run stays queued, the next drain runs it once and the promise resolves `{ ok: true, ran: true }`.
- `src/cron/service.run-queue.test.ts` › "reports a stream batch as consumed when its completion write meets a locked database": a real `CronService` run through `fireStreamJob`, with `cron.finalizeRuns` rejecting with `database is locked`. Before `4bda208` the fire rejects with that error (which the stream treats as a retryable lock); with it, it resolves `"fired"` and the payload ran once.
- Recovery without the test's explicit drain: the same drain-failure test with its `drainCronRunQueue(state)` call removed (a local, uncommitted variant; the committed test keeps the explicit drain to stay fast). The first `cron.drainQueue` after the forced run's commit rejects with `database is locked`, nothing else drains, and the run still completes once on its own at the scheduler's next timer pass (`MAX_CRON_TIMER_DELAY_MS` = 60 s):
  ```
  [trace] first drain rejected: database is locked; no explicit drain follows
  [trace] run settled {"ok":true,"ran":true} after 60041 ms; payload runs=1
   ✓ |cron| src/cron/service.run-queue.test.ts > keeps a committed manual run for the next drain when its drain meets a locked database 61078ms
  ```
- After `4bda208`: `service.run-queue`, `cron-stream-output` and `server-cron` tests pass (120 tests), plus `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:core:test`, oxlint, oxfmt and `pnpm check:import-cycles`.
- `pnpm test src/cron/service src/gateway/cron-stream-output.test.ts`: 58 cron files / 518 tests and 14 stream tests pass, except `ops.gateway-mutations.test.ts` › "leaves durable state unchanged when its caller is revoked during validation", which hit its 10 s `cron.add` request timeout while the host was loaded and passes when the file is run alone (11/11). `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:core:test`, oxlint and oxfmt on the changed files are clean.
- **Live proof (2026-10-30, isolated Gateway, this PR's head vs. its base `805891d`):**
  - Setup: an isolated Gateway built from this checkout (separate state dir and loopback port), a local OpenAI-compatible stub model, and a stream job created with the CLI: `openclaw cron add --stream-command '["bash","emit.sh","<trigger file>"]' --stream-mode match --stream-match '^turn ended' --session isolated --no-deliver`. `emit.sh` prints `turn ended …` when the trigger file appears. A separate process takes `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on the Gateway's `state/openclaw.sqlite` for 8 s and creates the trigger file 0.5 s later, so the batch's fire meets the lock (busy timeout 5 s). The result is read with `openclaw cron runs --json`, `openclaw cron list --json` and the Gateway log.
  - PR head: the fire is rejected before the run is requested, the batch is retried after the lock is released, and the job runs once:
    ```
    00:47:42.616 write lock acquired
    00:47:43.117 stream line triggered
    [sqlite/transaction] SQLite transaction lock wait failed ... operation=cron.schedule-unowned code=ERR_SQLITE_ERROR elapsedMs=5008 failureKind=lock-contention sqliteErrcode=5 step=begin
    00:47:48.482 WARN cron-stream: batch fire hit a locked database; retrying {"err":"Error: database is locked","attempt":1,"delayMs":5000}
    00:47:50.623 write lock released
    00:48:15.571 run finished: status ok (one run for this batch)
    state: streamStatus=running, no streamDroppedBatches
    ```
  - Base build (fresh state dir, same steps): the batch is lost, as in the field report above:
    ```
    00:57:29.003 write lock acquired
    00:57:29.504 stream line triggered
    00:57:34.804 WARN cron-stream: batch fire failed {"err":"Error: database is locked"}
    00:57:37.011 write lock released
    runs after 60 s: 0
    state: streamDroppedBatches=1
    ```
  - Completion write meets the lock (2026-10-30, `4bda208` vs. the previous head `d7aa4c6`, same setup; the stub model now records each request and waits 3 s). The lock script creates the trigger, waits until the payload's model request arrives, then holds `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` for 30 s, so the run finishes while the lock is held and its `cron.run-finalization` write fails:
    ```
    previous head d7aa4c6:
    02:54:58.043 payload started / write lock acquired
    [sqlite/transaction] ... operation=cron.run-finalization ... failureKind=lock-contention
    02:55:26.374 WARN cron: queued launch failed {"err":"Error: database is locked"}
    02:55:28.119 WARN cron-stream: batch fire hit a locked database; retrying {"attempt":1,"delayMs":5000}   <- consumed batch queued again
    this head 4bda208:
    02:43:46.809 payload started / write lock acquired
    [sqlite/transaction] ... operation=cron.run-finalization ... failureKind=lock-contention
    02:44:09.929 WARN cron: queued launch failed {"err":"Error: database is locked"}
    no cron-stream retry; payload executions for the batch: 1; streamDroppedBatches not incremented
    ```
    In both builds the job then stays marked running (`runningAtMs` set, no run-history entry) until receipt recovery, as described in the edge case above.
  - Gap: the drain-after-commit case is a window of milliseconds that an external lock holder cannot hit reliably, so it is covered by the unit test above, not by the live run.
- `cron-stream-output`, `cron-stream-output.interleavings`, `cron-stream-watchers`, `.cleanup` and `.extinction` pass: 63/63 with `vitest.gateway-core.config.ts`.
- Also run locally on the changed files: `tsgo -p tsconfig.core.json` (clean), `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint -c .oxlintrc.json` (clean).
- Reproduction outside the test suite: a second process holds `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on a temporary WAL database. `runSqliteImmediateTransactionSync` from the 2026.10.6 bundle then fails with the same `lock wait failed` fields: `nativeAttempts:1`, `nativeMs:5008`, errcode 5. With a 2 s hold it succeeds.

## Merge Danger

Two-way door: reverting restores the immediate drop. No persistent state or format changes. Blast radius is stream schedules whose fire rejects with SQLite BUSY/LOCKED.

The worst case is a delayed batch (about 90 s at the production cadence). The `requestManualCronRun` change also affects `openclaw cron run` and other manual callers: when the drain right after the commit fails, they now get the run's eventual result (or the enqueue acknowledgement) instead of an error for a run that still executes later.

prs.title: fix(agent): block direct openclaw cli state mutation in exec and prioritize messaging tools in code mode
prs.body:
Related: #187354

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Embedded agent runs in Code Mode (`tools.codeMode: 'auto'`) inside the Gateway container spawn the full `openclaw` CLI inside shell `exec` to manage cron and automations, triggering child process bootstrapping (~500MB+ RAM), SQLite database lease lock contention, container OOM kill (exit code 137), and an unverified completion message sent to end users upon restart recovery.

## User Impact

User impact: Prevents container OOM crashes and false-positive completion confirmations when users ask agents to schedule reminders or manage automations via chat/messaging channels. Models are steered immediately to use fast in-process async tool globals rather than launching the CLI binary as a subprocess, while remote node and sandbox CLI workflows remain preserved.

## Why This Change Was Made

In response to ClawSweeper architectural review feedback:
1. **Preserves CLI execution outside Gateway context:** Scopes the CLI footgun guard to Gateway execution (`host === "gateway"` or default). Legitimate CLI execution against external nodes (`host: 'node'`) or sandboxes (`host: 'sandbox'`) continues without restriction.
2. **Root-option-aware command parsing:** Reuses OpenClaw's `getRootOptionAwareCommandPath` to parse subcommands after global flags (e.g. `openclaw --no-color cron --help` and `openclaw --profile dev automations create`).
3. **Accurate tool remediation arguments:** Fixed remediation text to reference the actual `message: ...` parameter expected by `message({ action: 'send', target: ..., message: ... })`.
4. **Prioritizes messaging-critical tools in Code Mode:** Ensures `automations`, `cron`, and `message` are retained at priority 0 in `formatCodeModeCatalogIndex`.

## Evidence

- Unit tests in `src/infra/exec-control-command-guard.test.ts` verifying:
  - Gateway rejection of `openclaw cron --help` and root-option variants (`--no-color`, `--profile`).
  - Correct remediation message formatting with `message: ...`.
  - Preserved execution on `host: 'node'` and `host: 'sandbox'`.
- Unit tests in `src/agents/code-mode.test.ts` verifying catalog prioritization for `automations`, `cron`, and `message`.
- Grounded in production reproduction in OpenClaw 2026.10.8 (`openclaw-gateway` Docker image) documented in #187354:
  `Killed\n\n(Command exited with code 137)` following `await exec({ command: "openclaw cron --help" })`.

prs.title: fix: prevent startup rollback from hanging on usage backfill
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Gateway startup rollback can wait minutes for usage backfill after startup has already failed.

## User Impact

Usage backfill stops promptly while discovery or scan admission is pending. A CLI process that will exit after startup failure applies the existing shutdown cleanup grace; embedded hosts and recoverable in-process startup failures continue joining cleanup before reusing resources. Startup failures retain their original nonzero failure status.

No configuration, schema, stored-data, dependency, or version changes are required. Unfinished usage projections rebuild on the next startup. Native work and accepted writes still retain their existing settlement requirements; process-exiting rollback can report retained resources rather than certify a clean join.

## Why This Change Was Made

The usage lifetime already aborts its work scope, but startup roster discovery did not forward that signal to its shared-state read, and usage scans did not forward it while waiting for a cold database admission turn. The best-effort refresh-health enumeration now also observes its owning work scope.

The run loop explicitly supplies its startup-failure exit decision. Kernel rollback and outer reader/broker cleanup consume that decision through the existing cleanup owners and grace periods. Runtime ownership is retained when cleanup cannot join; recovery does not reuse that runtime. Replaced-installation refusal reporting and its boot completion fact now live with the existing restart-recovery reporter, keeping the main run loop at its original 1,274 counted lines.

## Evidence

Two regression groups fail against base `5ed97e5013787ed69be30c537c44e072188dfe35`: usage stop remains pending past 100 ms during discovery and scan admission; process-owned startup rollback remains pending past 10 seconds of simulated time. The embedded rollback control continues waiting correctly. All fixtures use isolated state and ports.

Final focused proof: 19 tests pass across the usage lifetime, startup lifetime, and Tailscale startup cleanup files (52.35 s wrapper wall time). The final CLI restart-cleanup and installation-replacement selection passes 21 cases (29.03 s wall time). Completed broader sibling groups totaled 146 passing cases, with 7 platform/runtime skips (overlaps the touched proof), covering usage workers, database admission, roster discovery, plugin state, and broker/shutdown ownership. Production and focused test typechecks, targeted lint, formatting, `git diff --check`, and the test-line, max-lines suppression, and line-growth ratchets pass. Net production LOC: +47; net test LOC: 0; docs: +5.

The broader CLI file exposed an inherited host limitation: package-handoff fixtures reject this checkout's group-writable external-volume ancestor as an unsafe temporary directory. The identical readiness failure reproduces on the pinned base (1 failed, 160 skipped); no permission guard, baseline, timeout, or mount permission was changed. The broad run was interrupted after the failed fixtures left it waiting at teardown; affected restart tests were rerun after updating the explicit close-option expectation and pass.

The production journal identifies the retained usage sidecar but does not identify the exact pending read behind the multi-minute delay. The regressions prove the uncancellable discovery and scan-admission windows. Native sections and accepted writes keep their existing settlement contracts. Independent autoreview and the landing decision remain with the coordinator under the work order. The worker will not merge.


## CI failure follow-up

Final head `9ee91e0ab3d623a2223bccc24396dfd6feb62bef` repairs the assertion-safety failure from [prior CI run 40947346971](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40947346971). The awaited plugin-state entries now bind to a local variable, placing the existing `SAFETY` comment immediately above its existing assertion. No new assertion or baseline entry was added. `nice -n 5 pnpm check:assertion-safety` passes with zero new violations (`2397 files, 5443 grandfathered assertions`); targeted lint, formatting, core typecheck, and the commit hook pass.

The MCP expiry failure in [`checks-node-changed-compact-small-16-3`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40947346971/job/123706983685) is classified **intermittent**, not proven inherited. The saved job log identifies `src/gateway/server.mcp-auth-login.test.ts` / `reports an expired attempt rather than an explicit cancellation`. The test passes on final branch sources and on freshly fetched main `642e1749d549d37e94f75eae89317db006f084b4` (one pass and 36 unselected tests each), followed by **10/10 additional passing executions on the branch** (143.48 s total wrapper time). Each execution used:

```sh
nice -n 5 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server.mcp-auth-login.test.ts --maxWorkers=8 -t 'reports an expired attempt rather than an explicit cancellation'
```

The main comparison used a detached isolated checkout, identical package manifests/lockfile, existing matching workspace dependencies, isolated test state, and the repository test wrapper. Two initial missing-workspace-dependency setup failures were corrected before the product test ran; neither counted as a test verdict. The comparison checkout was removed afterward. The passing local repetitions classify the observed failure; they do not establish a repair to the MCP expiry flow. No MCP code or test assertion changed, and CI was not rerun to chase green.

Ready for coordinator admin merge review at the final head, subject to the coordinator's fresh exact-head CI assessment. No merge performed.

prs.title: fix: shared-state policy errors can abort Gateway startup
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes shared-state schema-policy admission errors during Gateway startup when installation facts change while a cleanup client still retains the earlier database actor. The same error can prevent plugin state reads.

## User Impact

The shared-state owner closes and reopens its actor under the new policy without requiring plugin callers to manage database actors. Schemas, stored data, configuration, and migration rules are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Policy transitions closed only the owner's regular client. Lease cleanup can hold another client on that actor, leaving its original policy alive and making the next open fail with `Shared-state worker schema policy changed; close its actor first`.

Reuse the existing actor-wide retirement operation so every client drains before the replacement opens. Preserve the refusal for policy transitions inside retained owner operations, which must not wait on their own leases. The real-worker regression replaces a mocked quiescent-retirement test. Production LOC: +2; test LOC: -1.

## Evidence

- Exact-head [CI run 40945300534](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40945300534) completed successfully at `7750c74f8d08b6967a705e32f4625c329a913627`: 46 jobs successful, 28 skipped, zero failures. Current required `openclaw/ci-gate`: SUCCESS. PR remains ready and MERGEABLE. No CI reruns.
- Final regression is red on base `5ed97e5013787ed69be30c537c44e072188dfe35`: 1 failed, 1 passed, with the exact schema-policy error at broker admission. It opens a worker without installation facts, retains a cleanup client, then supplies the installation facts through the production context owner.
- `nice -n 5 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/sqlite-worker-existing-schema.test.ts src/state/worker-policy-regression-owner.test.ts src/state/openclaw-state-worker-lease.test.ts --maxWorkers=8`: 19 passed across 3 files; 35.94s including worker preparation. Unit shard 1.16s, infra shard 2.26s; infra test bodies 557ms and 315ms. Hosted CI workflow wall time: 22m57s; per-file CI timings were not separately collected.
- `nice -n 5 pnpm tsgo:core`: passed.
- `nice -n 5 node scripts/run-tsgo-core-test-shards.mjs --changed-paths-json '["src/infra/sqlite-worker-existing-schema.test.ts","src/state/worker-policy-regression-owner.test.ts"]'`: passed (state-logging graph). Existing advisory: 734 roots versus 720; no budget changed.
- Targeted `run-oxlint.mjs`, `pnpm format:check`, `git diff --check`, line-cap and max-lines ratchets: passed.

One earlier focused run hit a Bun SIGTRAP before collecting infra tests; the focused retry completed. No runtime or dependencies were changed. Proof uses isolated temporary databases and real worker actors; no live Gateway or user state was accessed. The incident log does not record the two competing policies, so the exact production interleaving remains unverified; this deterministically reproduces and fixes the retained-client ownership failure.

Operators cannot configure document attachments independently of a setting named for media.

prs.title: fix(gateway): strip __controlUiReconnectResume from chat.send params before validation
prs.body:
<!--
Closes: #165433
-->

## What Problem This Solves
Fixes: `chat.send` requests from non-Operator-UI clients (e.g. webchat on a browser reconnect with a preserved `sessionId`) are rejected with `invalid chat.send params: at root: unexpected property '__controlUiReconnectResume'`. `resolveControlUiReconnectResumeParams` only strips the internal `__controlUiReconnectResume` marker when both `value === true` AND `isOperatorUiClient(clientInfo)` returns true; in every other case the `__`-prefixed marker leaks into the AJV-strict `chat.send` schema and the request is dropped before dispatch.

## User Impact
User impact: Webchat and other browser-based reconnect paths that emit the internal `__controlUiReconnectResume` marker now have their messages admitted and dispatched normally on reconnect. No user-visible change for Control UI clients — their behavior is preserved.

## Why This Change Was Made
`__controlUiReconnectResume` is an internal `__`-prefixed wire field added by the Control UI to signal "treat this as a reconnect resume, not a fresh run." Such fields should never reach the public `chat.send` schema. The patch decouples "strip the field before validation" from "record that a resume was requested" — the field is now stripped whenever it is present on the input record, and the `resumeRequested` flag is still gated by both the strict-value check and the Operator UI client check, preserving the downstream semantics. The strict-value check is unchanged on purpose so a non-true value (e.g. `false`, `1`, the wrong type) still does not mark a resume even from an Operator UI client.

## Evidence
- Six focused unit tests added in `src/gateway/server-methods/chat-server-timing.test.ts` (new file) cover the regression and the surrounding cases: field absent, non-object input, true value with operator UI client, true value with non-operator UI client (the regression), true value with missing `clientInfo`, non-true values with operator UI client, and input-record immutability.
- A local reproduction on the bundled `dist/chat-server-timing-soo795Of.mjs` (the same logic, minified) confirmed the bug and the fix: pre-patch, a `webchat` clientInfo with `__controlUiReconnectResume: true` returned the marker in the result params; post-patch, the marker is stripped and `resumeRequested` is `false`.
- `diff -u` of the patched file vs. upstream main shows changes confined to the `resolveControlUiReconnectResumeParams` function body; no other exports, signatures, or unrelated fields are touched.

Closes #166729

## What Problem This Solves

Operators cannot declare their own decision endpoint, credentials, and model IDs through `models.providers`, even though that configuration flow supports custom chat providers.

## User Impact

Operators can declare `type: "decision"`, `decisionProvider`, `baseUrl`, an API key or SecretRef, and model IDs, then select `custom/model` with `decisionModel`. The installed adapter must support configured providers and the endpoint must implement its native protocol. TypeSafe supports this contract; ONNX's local model loader does not. Remote TypeSafe endpoints require HTTPS; explicit loopback HTTP is supported. Decision evidence goes to the configured endpoint.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bind custom provider identities to an installed plugin's wire adapter through an optional factory on the existing decision-provider contract. Keep aliases under that plugin's managed lifecycle, expose their models in the separate Decision catalog, exclude them from chat resolution, and invalidate evaluations and provider health when their configuration changes. Existing chat declarations keep their behavior.

The config documentation baseline grows by exactly two core fields (`type` and `decisionProvider`, 2495 → 2497). Both are necessary to distinguish the model role from the adapter that owns the endpoint protocol. No additional public SDK export is needed.

## Evidence

- Conflict resolution at `d482c46aec` integrates upstream `eb266d242d`, preserves upstream's removal of the old model-schema smoke tests, retains the 13 new decision-provider regressions in their own file, and regenerates the config baseline. All 43 affected tests pass (13 schema tests in 2.27 seconds and 30 startup/runtime/reload/adapter tests in 39.32 seconds, one worker). Config-doc verification, focused typed lint, production typechecking, and diff checks pass. Feature production code is unchanged; broader implementation validation below was completed at `b67cf02501` and is retained as prior-head evidence.
- Config, model selection, catalog, gateway reload, and managed decision-runtime regressions pass. Registration regressions reproduce duplicate-adapter and alias/name-collision failures before their fixes and pass afterward.
- All 95 TypeSafe tests and all 1,140 shared plugin contract tests pass. The final native-adapter/configured-host selection passes 112 tests with one worker in 27.07 seconds wall time.
- Production/test typechecks, core and extension typed lint, all selected changed-file guards, SDK export budget, config docs baseline, import boundaries, documentation examples, MDX, and links pass. Unused-export and lint findings were fixed and their affected gates rerun. Independent autoreview findings were fixed; the final runtime review has no actionable P0–P2 findings.
- Hosted ClawSweeper review remains on hold. Its sanitized failure artifact identifies the first finding as an unverified URI (`literal_not_reviewed`) in the [TypeSafe URL-rejection fixture](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d482c46aec35e7b31247847edd5b4a91c3641de9/extensions/typesafe/src/decisions.test.ts#L55). The fixture contains an explicitly synthetic password and verifies credential-bearing URLs are refused before dispatch. Its unchanged source blob is `500d21fdab6523027dd02c1c40579885ba66707d`. A maintainer must qualify the exact fixture in the separate review-bot policy and release the hold before requesting re-review; source updates alone do not release it. [Review workflow](https://github.com/openclaw/clawsweeper/actions/runs/37689055629).
- `pnpm build` passes on committed head `b67cf02501` in 178.20 seconds. The UI build reports a startup JS size advisory of 364.8 KiB gzip against a 364.7 KiB budget. Full repository and authenticated live endpoint tests were not run.
- The isolated TypeSafe entrypoint profile is qualified against the clean source and matching build: 155.2 MiB peak RSS, 109.5 MiB above the baseline, and 0.55 seconds CPU above the baseline. No extra public SDK export is introduced (3649 exports).

prs.title: fix(sessions): ground assistant transcript media refs before replay
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: in later turns, the model treats managed-media paths the assistant wrote itself as verified attachments, even when no trusted tool produced the file in that turn.

Related gaps this also closes:

- A persisted case or alias collision such as `Bash` or `Web_Search` inherited local-media trust on replay.
- A reused session manager kept its first run's trusted-tool set after the run's tools changed.
- A 100,000-entry structured media array made write-time authorization and replay scan the whole array.
- Many spellings still named a managed file without matching any root alias: dot segments, separator runs, percent escapes, NFC/NFD, a filename boundary that a later `..` discards, a root whose own path contains a space, a tab, LF or CR inside a `file:` URL (the URL parser deletes them), an authorized path followed by `/../..`, `~/...`, on Windows a drive path the URL parser and `path.win32` read differently (`~/...`, a rooted path with no drive, `C://...`, a `#` or `?` in a segment a later `..` discards), and an authorized `file:` or `media://inbound` reference followed by a tab, LF or CR that the resolver joins onto another stored file (`ok.png<TAB>.fake` opens `ok.png.fake`).

Grounding does not rewrite user-authored text or stored transcript rows. The channel replay byte budget also applies to retained user entries, as described below.

## User Impact

Later model turns no longer see fabricated managed-media paths as verified attachments. Exact trusted paths survive. Case-colliding tool results do not inherit trust. A reused manager honors both removal and restoration of trusted tools. A 100,000-element duplicate or rejected structured-media array stops after 64 raw inspections. Configured history limits above 128 keep working.

Three compatibility changes need maintainer acceptance; each is listed under "Open for maintainers" below:

- Channel replay history is capped at 32 KiB per entry and 128 KiB per read, after grounding.
- `media://inbound:<port>/...`, a bare `media://inbound:/...` and empty userinfo (`media://@inbound/...`) no longer resolve. Non-empty userinfo was already refused on `main`.
- The authorization marker is additive transcript metadata, and transcripts written before it replay under the existing core-name rule.

There is no SQLite schema version, migration, config/default or Gateway protocol change. The internal recent-text read of the session-history worker and the memory actor gains an optional request flag (`includeTurnMediaReferences`) and an optional result field (`turnMediaReferences`). The public `SessionRecentConversationText` type is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Authority stays with the production transcript writer, and verification stays with the media and replay owners. Before persisting, the guarded writer records the run's local-media authorization decision, using the trust set that the prepared agent session carries (`attempt-session-runtime-prepare.ts` hands it over). Before a local path enters channel history, replay checks it against that recorded decision, same-turn provenance and the managed media store.

Whether a spelling names a managed file is decided by the resolver's own parsers rather than a hand-written fold: WHATWG `URL` for a URI root, `path.win32.normalize` for a Windows drive root and `path.posix.normalize` for any other filesystem root, after expanding a leading `~` the way `resolveUserPath` does. That includes spellings that run past a token boundary. The same boundary walk decides where an authorized path ends. For `file:` URLs, the matcher also reads the text with tab, LF and CR deleted, as the URL parser does, keeps only the redactions that a deleted character makes possible, and maps them back to the original offsets.

Where an authorized reference is followed by a tab, LF or CR and more of the same token, text alone cannot say whether it is prose (`ok.png<LF>next line`) or another file (`ok.png<TAB>.fake`, which the URL parser reads as `ok.png.fake`). The scan reports the raw spellings a reader could stop at, and the media owner (`findUnverifiedJoinedMediaSpellings` in `media-reference.ts`) resolves each one through the same path that verifies same-turn references. If one opens a managed file no same-turn reference verified, the alias is redacted; a joined name the store does not hold stays prose. Probes are capped at 64 per entry, and an alias whose joined token runs past 4,096 characters or offers more than 8 places to stop is redacted. A run directly after the alias followed by `/` or `\` is not probed unless the rest of the token, read with the run deleted, holds a `..` segment: without one it is a path beneath the authorized regular file, which is how a list of paths one per line looks.

An authorized alias followed by more text is also checked for names the resolver keeps, including `ok.png .fake` and a directory named `ok.png<TAB>`. `findRefusedMediaContinuations` reads the alias's directory, probes plausible other names, and refuses the alias when the listing fails or the placement/probe budget runs out. The resolver-to-replay case opens the other files, verifies redaction, removes those files, and verifies the same text then survives as prose.

The shared extractor has separate limits for accepted references and for raw structured candidates, and writer authorization and replay both apply the existing 64-reference policy to each.

Channel replay (`mergeSessionTranscriptContext`) opts into a byte budget applied after grounding: 32 KiB per retained entry and 128 KiB per read. Provenance readers do not. `session-upstream-monitor.ts` compares complete prompt text, and the plugin-SDK export returns complete text, as on `main`.

Selection is `main`'s single-snapshot reader, `readRecentTranscriptConversationText` (#169619). It runs inside one transcript snapshot in the session-history worker, the read-only reader and the memory actor, so it runs off the Gateway thread and through the actor that holds an incognito session. This PR adds an opt-in `includeTurnMediaReferences` option to it.

The reader walks the snapshot newest first. Each selected assistant entry collects the earlier rows of its own turn, stopping at the turn's user row and keeping at most 1,000 rows. The managed media that those rows' trusted tool results named come back on the entry as `turnMediaReferences`, capped by the same 64-reference policy. If the requested entries are already found but the oldest selected reply has not reached its turn start, the reader keeps paging until it does. Rows and their provenance therefore come from one snapshot. There is no page-to-page snapshot comparison, no retry and no provenance drop. Readers that do not set the option get `main`'s result unchanged.

The collector lives in `transcript-turn-media-references.ts`. `transcript-recent-grounding.ts` keeps grounding and the replay budget. `transcript.ts` requests the references through `main`'s worker-read entry and `assertCurrent`, then grounds. `main` moved the reader out of `transcript.ts`, which is now 639 counted lines against `main`'s 628, and the line-cap ratchet passes.

## Evidence

### Shipped Gateway proof at `d929366aca6c`, October 26

Built `d929366aca6c0a79b980ffdd2d3225e9a6925520` on macOS arm64 with Node `24.22.1`, pnpm `12.15.0`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` and `pnpm build qaRuntime`, followed by the full rebuild `scripts/run-node.mjs` started on its own (`dist is stale: missing_private_qa_dist`); `dist/index.js` SHA-256 `b94167b331b542449a2775ac3d44bb7ffb353bc9bfa71a51b5cf036557848254`. The checkout also carried #168611's four `qa-lab` files, which this Gateway does not load: `plugins.allow` is `telegram` plus the fixture below. Every run had its own throwaway HOME, state and config, started `node dist/index.js gateway run --bind loopback`, and drove the real Telegram plugin against a loopback Bot API stub, with a loopback scripted Responses provider as the model. No credentials or external endpoints.

A run-owned, non-bundled fixture plugin registers a speech provider, so the core `tts` tool runs and writes under `media/tool-speech-synthesis/`. The same plugin registers `music_generate`. No music provider is configured, so that tool is the plugin's, under a core name.

**Trusted path, core-named plugin and trust withdrawal.** 18:32:17 to 18:36:24 UTC, 10 of 10 checks passed. Five DMs in one Telegram session:

1. A: the model calls `tts` and `music_generate`, then replies with both managed paths and an unmanaged control path.
2. B: a plain turn, whose provider request is checked.
3. `tools.deny: ["tts"]` is written to the config file. The running Gateway accepts the revision without a restart, and turn C's provider requests carry no `tts` tool.
4. C: `music_generate` returns the file A's `tts` call wrote, and the reply names it twice.
5. The deny is removed. Turn D's requests offer `tts` again, and it writes a new file.
6. E: a plain turn, whose provider request is the final check.

The channel-history block ("Conversation context") of turn E's provider request, file names shortened:

```text
OpenClaw: AUTH-A trusted <state>/media/tool-speech-synthesis/voice---6780415c-....wav plugin [unverified media reference removed]/generated/upg-core-named.mp3 unmanaged /tmp/upg-unmanaged.txt
User: AUTH-B Reply exactly: AUTH-B
OpenClaw: AUTH-B
User: AUTH-C make a melody from the earlier note
OpenClaw: AUTH-C withdrawn [unverified media reference removed]/tool-speech-synthesis/voice---6780415c-....wav stale [unverified media reference removed]/tool-speech-synthesis/voice---6780415c-....wav
User: AUTH-D please speak another note
OpenClaw: AUTH-D restored <state>/media/tool-speech-synthesis/voice---c0eaa749-....wav
```

Turn B's request already showed A's line exactly as above. The persisted tool results, read from the stopped Gateway's database:

```text
seq  6  tts             voice---6780415c-....wav        localMediaReplayAuthorized=true
seq  9  music_generate  generated/upg-core-named.mp3    localMediaReplayAuthorized=false
seq 19  music_generate  voice---6780415c-....wav        localMediaReplayAuthorized=false
seq 26  tts             voice---c0eaa749-....wav        localMediaReplayAuthorized=true
```

The trusted path survives the final request. The core-named plugin's path does not. A result written while `tts` was withdrawn gets no authority, even for the file a trusted call produced in an earlier turn, and that earlier row keeps its own authority through the withdrawal and the restoration.

The withdrawal is an operator `tools.deny`. The plugin tool registry refuses a plugin tool whose name collides with a core tool that exists (`plugin tool name conflict`), and core `tts` is always constructed, so I found no shipped way to keep the same `tts` name callable while it loses trust.

Scope: the same final request also carries the session's own earlier assistant messages as `assistant` input items, unchanged. Items 6 and 12 of turn E hold the A and C replies with every path as written. This PR grounds the channel-history block and does not rewrite stored transcript rows, as described above.

**Upgrade from latest stable 2026.10.7.** 17:56:09 to 18:09:07 UTC. `npm view openclaw dist-tags` reported `latest: 2026.10.7` on October 26. Installed the published package into a throwaway prefix. npm 11.19.1 skipped dependency install scripts, so I ran the package's own `scripts/postinstall-bundled-plugins.mjs` (exit 0); `koffi`'s native install did not run.

1. 2026.10.7's Gateway (`node openclaw.mjs gateway run`) ran turn UPG-1, with the same tools plus a forged managed path (a real file in `media/inbound/` that no tool produced), and turn UPG-2. Its own replay kept all four paths as written. It left agent schema 25, global schema 20, 16 transcript rows and 1 session, and did not change the config file (SHA-256 `0d5596706adc` before and after).
2. With the Gateway stopped, the PR head's `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive` exited 0 and migrated agent schema 25 -> 33 and global schema 20 -> 31.
3. The PR head's Gateway then ran UPG-3 to UPG-5 on the same state and config.

```text
2026.10.7 replay, UPG-2 request:
  UPG-1 trusted <state>/media/tool-speech-synthesis/voice---1f778f68-....wav plugin <state>/media/generated/upg-core-named.mp3 forged <state>/media/inbound/upg-forged.png unmanaged /tmp/upg-unmanaged.txt
PR head replay of that 2026.10.7 row, UPG-3 request:
  UPG-1 trusted <state>/media/tool-speech-synthesis/voice---1f778f68-....wav plugin <state>/media/generated/upg-core-named.mp3 forged [unverified media reference removed]/inbound/upg-forged.png unmanaged /tmp/upg-unmanaged.txt
PR head replay of its own row, UPG-5 request:
  UPG-4 trusted <state>/media/tool-speech-synthesis/voice---dde2ff13-....wav plugin [unverified media reference removed]/generated/upg-core-named.mp3
```

- Transcript rows: all 16 rows written by 2026.10.7 are byte-identical after the PR head ran (SHA-256 of each stored row; 33 rows now), and the session key is still there.
- Settings: none of the 36 config values written for 2026.10.7 changed or disappeared. Doctor added 15 entries: migration and wizard stamps, `agents.defaults.modelPolicy.allow`, `agents.entries.main`, `channels.telegram.accounts.proof.groupAllowFrom: ["*"]`, `messages.queue.allowCollaborativeSteering: false`, and four disabled `skills.entries`. The harness's whole-file equality check reports FAIL for that reason; the other 9 checks passed.
- The 2026.10.7 row's `music_generate` path replays because rows without the marker fall back to the core-name rule, one of the open decisions below. The forged path is redacted because no tool result in its turn named it.

A first attempt skipped doctor. On the unmigrated 2026.10.7 state the PR head's Gateway did not answer `/readyz` within 600 s and logged `Sessions remain unavailable. Stop the Gateway, run "openclaw doctor --fix"`. This PR changes nothing under `src/state`, and base `794d6500f382` already declares agent schema 33.

`openclaw qa suite --channel-driver crabline` with an equivalent scenario did not get past Gateway startup here: the QA harness's 120 s listen deadline expired twice at load average 150 to 320, so the runs above use a 600 s readiness wait instead. Both runs used harness `proof-101866-gateway.mjs`, SHA-256 `601a1a62e0efc521cba2bfb238c11615da5fbe3393181d5c29ca9db3eeb7b41f`. Raw harness logs: authority `87cb7047de800e0e2a244b6772a46a6b9723f76342211e986348fee20e5f3d17`, upgrade `98ae49f309bf62a2122b7a38ad8d1fd215388e792d75d6b5302c7087f6de400d`. Every Gateway exited 0 on SIGTERM.

### Current-head validation

At [`d929366aca6c`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/d929366aca6c0a79b980ffdd2d3225e9a6925520), merged main `794d6500f382311cab58f5d474a9ef248598e5f2` without rebasing. The merge keeps `boundReplayBytes` with main's delivered-message context flags and keeps the media-grounding probes with main's classifier declarations. Tree: `aa78156fab9d9b6b0b39a17d19b130816a077b89`.

The Bun history-cache failure is present on the exact CI base without this PR. The same five-file group, Node `24.22.1`, Bun `1.4.4-canary.1+ef37c31de`, pnpm `12.15.0`, frozen installs, Linux x64, one worker:

| Source | Result |
| --- | --- |
| CI base `70b25401a70afe25917ce312aaaed15a63d212cb` | 66 passed, 1 failed, exit 1 |
| CI checkout `d7e301ea1098622ce6eb88e99f240a758814bb36` | 66 passed, 1 failed, exit 1 |
| Current head `d929366aca6c0a79b980ffdd2d3225e9a6925520` | 67 passed, 0 failed, exit 0 |

The candidate uses main's lockfile, including Vitest `5.0.5`; the historical controls use `5.0.3`. This comparison measures the complete integration.

Both failures are `session-accessor.sqlite-history-cache.test.ts:157`, `expected [] to have a length of 1 but got +0`, matching [job 120036958812](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39839421182/job/120036958812). All tracked source blobs matched the selected trees before running. Main already contains the cache's retained pressure channel in [ca3f7433914a](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/ca3f7433914ad35dda0ce39206b05845f23556e5); this merge carries that fix, with no separate cache patch.

Current-head focused results: **276 passed, 1 skipped across 14 files**. The groups were the CI configuration group (67), grounding and turn provenance (137), media helpers/comparison (25), channel context (9), and guarded-writer/session preparation (38). The skipped case is [`normalizeMediaReferenceForComparison > matches Windows network file URLs across scheme casing`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d929366aca6c0a79b980ffdd2d3225e9a6925520/src/media/media-reference-comparison.test.ts#L28), restricted by `it.runIf(process.platform === "win32")`. These runs were on Linux; they do not establish Windows behavior.

The [space-continuation regression](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d929366aca6c0a79b980ffdd2d3225e9a6925520/src/config/sessions/transcript-grounding.test.ts#L248) passes. Disabling only the continuation store probes makes that same case fail at line 310: the three `ok.png .fake` spellings and the tab-named directory replay verbatim instead of being redacted. The prose controls remain unchanged. Restored the production file and verified its SHA-256 returned to `cc9c6abaa1dd4d7b10ac67df45633007aa81668cf5bdd36a23b1690fdf1b9970`.

Reproduction of the five-file comparison, from each named tree with its frozen dependencies and the pinned Bun fork selected:

```sh
OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=bun node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run \
  --config test/vitest/vitest.runtime-config.config.ts \

```

The other groups used the same wrapper, Bun selection, and worker flags with these files:

```text

  src/config/sessions/transcript-grounding.unit.test.ts
  src/config/sessions/transcript-grounding.test.ts

media:
  src/media/media-reference.test.ts
  src/media/media-reference-comparison.test.ts

  src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.tools.media.test.ts

```

Oxfmt/Bun parity and scoped oxlint pass for the two conflict resolutions. Core typecheck passes: `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core.tsbuildinfo`. Independent source review against `794d6500f382311cab58f5d474a9ef248598e5f2` found no P0-P2 findings; it did not execute the project. All 59,191 tracked blobs matched the reviewed tree after validation and mutation restoration.

Hosted [CI run 40123672646](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40123672646) completed: **79 successful jobs, 26 skipped, 0 failed**. The [CI gate job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40123672646/job/120966132635) and the separate `openclaw/ci-gate`, `openclaw/dependency-review`, and `openclaw/security-sensitive-review` commit statuses are successful. At 19:31 UTC on October 24, all 18 workflows on this head were terminal: 16 successful and 2 skipped; all 161 check-runs were terminal: 105 successful, 55 skipped and 1 neutral.

The [preflight](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40123672646/job/120960427686) checked out merge `4efc146f92780a56604d80565c3b2d6d04c0a35b`, tree `b80612f193e208ad5870d32a6ba4aa3fa47be2e4`, with parents main `820c30a3a0101abd0a739406a116a95e1e99429d` and this head. That base is newer than the main commit used for the focused local validation. The complete CI log archive is 9,191,036 bytes, 944 members, CRC verified, SHA-256 `1239613479a3242f4fe70f099216bc946bb3008b975e6535ad7819999832832b`. In [job 120960718369](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40123672646/job/120960718369), Bun passed `SQLite transcript history cache > reuses recent payloads with fresh result ownership until append or rewrite` and `readRecentUserAssistantTextForSession grounding > refuses an authorized reference a space continues onto another stored file`.

The compatibility decisions below remain open. Current security requirements are evaluated by the [security-review workflow](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40123520186).

**Earlier measurements, on the older heads named below:**

Head `0ff83d79b6c` on an M4 Pro, with each file run on its own. The head merges `main` `e69e34001fb5` at `62dd1ca78a2`, then moves selection onto `main`'s single-snapshot reader.
